extraction_notes.note: The proof of Theorem 1.1 is running prose spread over Sections 5.2-5.4 and crosses subsection headings. Following 'a proof continued elsewhere', it is split into one proof node per subsection, each with a proves edge to TP4, and the later parts carry uses edges to the first. The intermediate facts '(K,d) is BPI' and '(K,d) does not look down on (H,d_b)' are not stated as separate sentences, so they stay inside the proof parts.

Theorem 1.3 has no proof environment. Section 3 builds the construction, Section 3.3 argues Ahlfors regularity and Section 3.4 argues 'no biLipschitz pieces'. These are two prose proof parts proving TP9, and the construction sentences are definitions.

'Let us show that K has nonempty interior' is followed by the argument. The claim node is the concluding 'Therefore ... nonempty interior' sentence, and the argument before it is a prose proof. The following Ahlfors-4-regularity sentence is a separate claim with no argument.
Numbered equation (2.4) is retyped as an external theorem because the text calls it Magnani's area formula.

These are short prose assertions with inline justification ('Lemma 3.3 holds in (K,d) as its proof only requires...'; the triangle inequality for d_b). Each was typed claim or remark by whether the argument is separable from the assertion.

Several passages got no node because they repeat formal content: the restatement of Theorem 1.5 at the start of Section 6.2, the intro's informal descriptions of BPI spaces, BPI equivalence and looking down, and the section-overview paragraphs of Sections 3, 5 and 6. 'Question 24 of Heinonen-Semmes' is only named and never stated, so it is not a node.

The source has a stray non-UTF character right after the eqnarray (6.1) in the proof of Theorem 1.4. Because of it, the finishing step warns that the step starting 'Indeed,' starts mid-sentence. The warning is a false alarm and was left.

The finishing step warns that the term 'self-similar' in ClP8 has no edge from DP4. It is left without an edge on purpose: ClP8 means the self-similar structure of the set K, not the self-similar distance that DP4 defines.

nodes.name: BPI equivalence implies look-down equivalence
nodes.statement: BPI equivalence of spaces $X$ and $Y$ implies that $X$ and $Y$ are \emph{look-down equivalent}, meaning that $X$ looks down on $Y$ and $Y$ looks down on $X$.
conclusions: $X$ and $Y$ are \emph{look-down equivalent}

nodes.name: Laakso's theorem (look-down equivalence does not imply BPI equivalence)
nodes.statement: However, Laakso has shown that the converse is not true in general \cite{laakso-bpi}.
nodes.statement_short: Look-down equivalent BPI spaces need not be BPI equivalent.
conclusions: the converse is not true in general

nodes.name: Minimal in looking down
nodes.statement: A space $X$ is \emph{mimimal} in looking down if every space $Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$.
differentia: every space $Y$ on which $X$ looks down is look-down equivalent to $X$

nodes.name: Kirchheim's theorem: Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down
nodes.statement: For example, from the result of Kirchheim \cite{Kirchheim} we know that Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down.
conclusions: Euclidean spaces are minimal in looking down

nodes.name: Quantitative Kirchheim theorem (Schul)
nodes.statement: A quantitative version of Kirchheim's theorem was later given in \cite{Schul_BiLipschitz_Decomposition} in which it was shown that if a map $f : [0,1]^n \to X$ has positive Hausdorff $n$-content, then it has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece.
nodes.statement_short: A map from the cube with positive Hausdorff $n$-content has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece.
assumptions: a map $f : [0,1]^n \to X$ has positive Hausdorff $n$-content
conclusions: it has a quantitatively large biLipschitz piece

nodes.name: David-Semmes Problem 11.15 (Heinonen-Semmes Question 22)
nodes.statement: David and Semmes asked in Problem 11.15 of \cite{davsem} if the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is also minimal in looking down, when equipped with sub-Riemannian distances, also called Carnot-Carath\'eodory distances. This was also asked as Question 22 of \cite{Heinonen_Semmes}.
nodes.origin_citation: David & Semmes, Problem 11.15; Heinonen & Semmes, Question 22
nodes.statement_short: Is the sub-Riemannian Heisenberg group minimal in looking down?

nodes.name: Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down
nodes.statement: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down.
conclusions: The subRiemannian Heisenberg group is not minimal in looking down.
nodes.label: thm:Hnotminimal

nodes.name: Countably n-rectifiable metric measure space
nodes.statement: Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is countably $n$-rectifiable if there exist a countable set of Borel subsets $A_i \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and Lipschitz maps $f : A_i \to X$ such that $\mu\left(X \backslash \bigcup_i f(A_i) \right) = 0$ and $\mu \ll \mathcal H^n$ where $\mathcal H^n$ is the Hausdorff $n$-measure.
differentia: there exist a countable set of Borel subsets $A_i \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and Lipschitz maps $f : A_i \to X$ such that $\mu\left(X \backslash \bigcup_i f(A_i) \right) = 0$ and $\mu \ll \mathcal H^n$

nodes.name: Kirchheim's biLipschitz decomposition of rectifiable sets
nodes.statement: It was shown in \cite{Kirchheim} that, by further countably decomposing each $f(A_i)$ if necessary, one may assume that each $f_i$ is biLipschitz.
conclusions: one may assume that each $f_i$ is biLipschitz

nodes.name: H-rectifiability
nodes.statement: One can easily create a definition of being $\mathbb H$-rectifiable by letting each $A_i$ be a Borel subset of the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ and setting $n = 4$, the Hausdorff dimension of $\mathbb H$.

nodes.name: Lipschitz H-rectifiability is strictly weaker than biLipschitz H-rectifiability
nodes.statement: However, we now see that there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$.
nodes.statement_short: Some positive-measure Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ is not a countable union of biLipschitz images.
conclusions: there exists a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ with positive Hausdorff 4-measure that is the Lipschitz image of a subset of $\mathbb H$ but is not the countable union of biLipschitz images of subsets of $\mathbb H$

nodes.name: Shortened Ahlfors-regular distance on the Heisenberg group
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group. There exists a distance $d$ on $\mathbb H $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq d_{cc}$; \item $(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular; \item if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: There is a distance $d\le d_{cc}$ on $\mathbb H$, Ahlfors 4-regular, not biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$ on any set of positive measure.
assumptions: Let $(\mathbb H, d_{cc})$ be the subRiemannian Heisenberg group.
conclusions: $d\leq d_{cc}$
$(\mathbb H, d)$ is Ahlfors 4-regular
if $A\subseteq \mathbb H$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^4_{cc}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $d_{cc}$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.label: thm:Heisenbergdistance

nodes.name: Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to Carnot groups have biLipschitz pieces
nodes.statement: Indeed, one can then use a similar argument as in \cite{Kirchheim}, with inspiration from \cite{pauls}, to show that Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to another Carnot group with positive 4-measure image have biLipschitz pieces.
assumptions: Lipschitz maps from the Heisenberg group to another Carnot group with positive 4-measure image
conclusions: have biLipschitz pieces

nodes.name: G.C. David's biLipschitz pieces theorem
nodes.statement: Another situation where Lipschitz maps have biLipschitz pieces is when the spaces are Ahlfors regular, linearly locally contractible topological manifolds and the target has manifold weak tangents, see the work of G.C. David \cite{gcdavid} (this David is not the same David of David-Semmes).
assumptions: the spaces are Ahlfors regular, linearly locally contractible topological manifolds and the target has manifold weak tangents
conclusions: Lipschitz maps have biLipschitz pieces

nodes.name: The space (H,d) has no manifold tangents
nodes.statement: We note that in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} the constructed space $(\mathbb H, d)$ neither has manifold tangents nor is linearly locally contractible.

nodes.name: Shortcut distance on Ahlfors-regular spaces (general theorem)
nodes.statement: Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and $Q>0$. Assume \begin{enumerate} \item $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$ and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r). \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Then there exists a distance $d$ on $X $ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $d\leq \rho$; \item $(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular; \item if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: If an Ahlfors $Q$-regular space admits shortcuts at every scale, there is a smaller Ahlfors $Q$-regular distance biLipschitz to the original on no positive-measure set.
assumptions: Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and $Q>0$.
there exists $\lambda\in(0,1)$ such that for all $p\in X$ and all $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there exist $q_1, q_2\in B_\rho (p,r)$ such that $$\rho(q_1, q_2) \geq \lambda r$$
conclusions: $d\leq \rho$;
$(X, d)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular;
if $A\subseteq X$ is a subset with $\mathcal H^Q_{\rho}(A)>0$, then $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.label: thm:general

nodes.name: Shortcut assumption (1.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(p_1, p_2) \leq \rho (p_1, q_1) + \rho (p_2, q_2), \qquad \forall p_1, p_2 \notin B_\rho (p,r).
nodes.label: e:general-metric-assumption

nodes.name: Biased-down left-biLipschitz distances are locally biLipschitz to d_cc
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be a distance on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ such that $d \le d_{cc}$ and $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$. Assume that the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$. Then $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.
nodes.statement_short: A distance $d\le d_{cc}$ with biLipschitz left translations and positive $\mathcal H^4_d$ of the unit ball is biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$ on compacts.
assumptions: Assume that the left translations in $\mathbb H$ are biLipschitz with respect to $d$.
conclusions: Then $d$ and $ d_{cc}$ are biLipschitz equivalent on compact sets.
nodes.label: thm:positiveinvarianttobilip

nodes.name: Necessity of the assumptions of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: We remark that the assumptions in Theorem~\ref{thm:positiveinvarianttobilip} are necessary. Indeed, if we don't assume $d \le d_{cc}$, then as a counterexample one can take two sub-Riemannian distances on $\mathbb H$ that have two different horizontal bundles. If we don't assume $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{cc}(0,1))> 0$, then a counterexample is given by every Riemannian left-invariant distance. Moreover, the distance $\min\{1, d_{cc}\}$ shows that the conclusion of the theorem may not be global.
nodes.statement_short: Dropping $d\le d_{cc}$ or the positive-measure hypothesis breaks Theorem 1.4, and $\min\{1,d_{cc}\}$ shows the conclusion is only local.

nodes.name: Kirchheim's metric differentiation theorem
nodes.statement: Kirchheim's result in \cite{Kirchheim} can be stated as the fact that every semi-distance $d$ in $\mathbb R^n$ that is smaller than the Euclidean distance is metrically differentiable, i.e., at almost every point its blow-up is a homogeneous semi-distance.
assumptions: every semi-distance $d$ in $\mathbb R^n$ that is smaller than the Euclidean distance
conclusions: is metrically differentiable, i.e., at almost every point its blow-up is a homogeneous semi-distance

nodes.name: Pauls' horizontal metric differentiation on Carnot groups
nodes.statement: Similarly, by \cite{Pauls01}, we know that on Carnot groups semi-distances smaller than $ d_{cc}$ are metrically differentiable but only in the horizontal directions.
assumptions: on Carnot groups semi-distances smaller than $ d_{cc}$
conclusions: are metrically differentiable but only in the horizontal directions

nodes.name: Kirchheim-Magnani counterexample to metric differentiability
nodes.statement: Regarding non-horizontal directions, from \cite{Kirchheim_Magnani} we know that there is a distance in the Heisenberg group that is a counterexample to metric differentiability, although it is not biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$.
conclusions: there is a distance in the Heisenberg group that is a counterexample to metric differentiability

nodes.name: Self-similar (semi-)distance
nodes.statement: If $\{\delta_\lambda\}_{\lambda>0}$ denotes the standard one-paramenter family of isomorphisms of $\mathbb H $, see Section \ref{sec:Heis}, a (semi-)distance $d$ is {\em self-similar} if there exists some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $.
differentia: there exists some $\lambda>1$ for which $d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q)$, for all $p,q\in \mathbb H $

nodes.name: Blow-up of a distance
nodes.statement: In the following result, by {\em a blow-up} of a distance $d$ we mean any pointwise limit of the functions \[(p_1,p_2)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d( q_j \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_1), q_j \delta_{\lambda_j} ( p_2)) ,\] as $\lambda_j \to 0$ and $q_j\in \mathbb H $.
nodes.statement_short: A blow-up of $d$ is any pointwise limit of rescaled translated copies $\lambda_j^{-1}d(q_j\delta_{\lambda_j}\cdot,q_j\delta_{\lambda_j}\cdot)$ with $\lambda_j\to0$.

nodes.name: Failure of Kirchheim-metric differentiation for biLipschitz maps
nodes.statement: There exist two distances $d_1, d_2$ on $\mathbb H $ that are biLipschitz equivalent to $d_{cc}$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar. \item No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Two distances biLipschitz to $d_{cc}$: one left-invariant with no self-similar blow-up, one with no left-invariant or self-similar blow-up.
conclusions: There exist two distances $d_1, d_2$ on $\mathbb H $ that are biLipschitz equivalent to $d_{cc}$
The distance $d_1$ is left-invariant, but no blow-up of $d_1$ is self-similar.
No blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant nor self-similar.
nodes.label: thm:fail

nodes.name: Hausdorff Q-measure
nodes.statement: Let $Q > 0$. Then for $A \subseteq X$, one defines \[ \mathcal H^Q_d(A) := \lim_{s \to 0^+} \inf \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^\infty (\operatorname{diam} E_i)^Q : A \subseteq \bigcup_i E_i \text{ an open cover}, \operatorname{diam}(E_i) < s\right\}. \] We say that $\mathcal H^Q$ is the Hausdorff $Q$-measure of $(X,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hausdorff $Q$-measure via covers by sets of small diameter.

nodes.name: Hausdorff measure is Borel regular
nodes.statement: It is known that the Hausdorff $Q$-measure is Borel regular although it may not be locally finite.
conclusions: the Hausdorff $Q$-measure is Borel regular although it may not be locally finite

nodes.name: Ahlfors Q-regular metric measure space
nodes.statement: Let $Q > 0$. Recall that a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is said to be Ahlfors $Q$-regular if there exists $C \geq 1$ so that \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\operatorname{diam} X}{2}.\]
differentia: there exists $C \geq 1$ so that \[\frac{1}{C} r^Q \leq \mu(B(x,r)) \leq C r^Q, \qquad \forall x \in X, r < \frac{\operatorname{diam} X}{2}.\]

nodes.name: Ahlfors regularity passes to Hausdorff measure
nodes.statement: We remark that if $(X,d,\mu)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular, then $(X,d,\mathcal H^Q)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular.
conclusions: $(X,d,\mathcal H^Q)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular

nodes.name: C-conformally biLipschitz map with scale factor
nodes.statement: A biLipschitz map $f$ between metric spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ is said to be $C$-{\em conformally biLipschitz} with scale factor $\lambda > 0$ if $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$.
differentia: $f$ is $C$-biLipschitz between the metric spaces $(X, \lambda d)$ and $(X',d')$

nodes.name: BPI space
nodes.statement: An Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space $(X,d)$ is said to be a \emph{BPI} (``big pieces of itself'') {\em space} if there exist constants $C \ge 1$ and $\theta > 0$ such that for all $x_1,x_2 \in X$ and $0 < r_1 , r_2 < \operatorname{diam}(X)$ there is a closed set $A \subseteq B(x_1,r_1)$ with $\mathcal{H}^Q(A) \ge \theta r_1^Q$ and if there is a $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x_2,r_2)$ with scale factor $r_2/r_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Any two balls contain a big closed subset of one that embeds conformally biLipschitz into the other.
nodes.label: def:BPI

nodes.name: BPI equivalence
nodes.statement: Two BPI spaces $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ of the same dimension $Q$ are called \emph{BPI equivalent} if there exist constants $\theta>0$ and $C>0$ such that for each $x \in X$, $x' \in X'$ and radii $0 < R < \operatorname{diam}(X)$, $0 < R' < \operatorname{diam}(X')$ there exist a subset $A \subset B(x,R) \subset X$ with $\mathcal H^Q_d(A)\ge \theta R^Q$ and an $C$-conformally biLipschitz embedding $f \colon A \to B(x',R')$ with scale factor $R'/R$.
nodes.statement_short: Big pieces of balls of one space embed conformally biLipschitz into balls of the other, uniformly.

nodes.name: Looking down (look-down equivalence)
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ and $(X',d')$ be BPI metric spaces of Hausdorff dimension $Q$. The space $(X,d)$ is said to \emph{look down on} $(X',d')$ if there is a closed set $A \subset X$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon A \to X'$ such that $f(A)$ has positive Hausdorff $Q$-measure. If also $X'$ looks down on $X$, then $X$ and $X'$ are called \emph{look-down equivalent}.
nodes.statement_short: $X$ looks down on $X'$ if a Lipschitz map from a closed subset of $X$ has image of positive $\mathcal H^Q$-measure.

nodes.name: Heisenberg group
nodes.statement: The Heisenberg group $\mathbb H$ is the simply connected Lie group whose Lie algebra is generated by three vectors $X,Y,Z$ with only non-zero relation $[X,Y]=Z$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
differentia: whose Lie algebra is generated by three vectors $X,Y,Z$ with only non-zero relation $[X,Y]=Z$

nodes.name: Heisenberg group law in exponential coordinates
nodes.statement: Via exponential coordinates it can be identified as the manifold $\mathbb R^3$ equipped with Lie multiplication: \[ p\cdot q = \left( x_p + x_q, y_p + y_q, z_p + z_q + \frac12 (x_py_q - y_px_q) \right). \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Identity and center of the Heisenberg group
nodes.statement: It follows easily from the definition that the origin $(0,0,0) \in \mathbb H$ is the identity element and that the center of the group is \[ {\rm Z}({\mathbb H}) = \{(0,0,z) : z \in \mathbb R\}. \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
conclusions: the origin $(0,0,0) \in \mathbb H$ is the identity element
the center of the group is \[ {\rm Z}({\mathbb H}) = \{(0,0,z) : z \in \mathbb R\}. \]

nodes.name: Heisenberg dilations
nodes.statement: For each $\lambda > 0$, the Heisenberg group has an automorphism defined as \begin{equation} \delta_\lambda (x,y,z) := (\lambda x, \lambda y, \lambda^2 z). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Dilation formula (2.1)
nodes.statement: \delta_\lambda (x,y,z) := (\lambda x, \lambda y, \lambda^2 z).
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.label: hom:dil

nodes.name: Homogeneous (semi-)distance
nodes.statement: A left-invariant (semi-)distance $d$ is {\em homogeneous}, with respect to \eqref{hom:dil}, if for all $\lambda>0$ \begin{equation} d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q\in \mathbb H. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Homogeneity (2.2)
nodes.statement: d(\delta_\lambda (p),\delta_\lambda (q)) =\lambda d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q\in \mathbb H.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.label: eq:homog:dist

nodes.name: Box norm
nodes.statement: We introduce the {\em box norm} \[ \norm{p} := \max\left\{|x_p|,|y_p|, \sqrt{|z_p|}\right\}. \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Box distance
nodes.statement: We define the {\em box distance} as \[ d_b(p,q) := \norm{p^{-1}q}. \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Box distance is left-invariant and homogeneous
nodes.statement: Clearly, $d_b$ is left-invariant and it satisfies \eqref{eq:homog:dist}.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
conclusions: $d_b$ is left-invariant and it satisfies \eqref{eq:homog:dist}

nodes.name: Jacobian of a homomorphism
nodes.statement: Given a homomorphism $L : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$, one can define the Jacobian to be \[ J(L) = \frac{\mathcal H^4_{d_b}(L(B_{d_b}(0,1)))}{\mathcal H_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,1))}. \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances

nodes.name: Pansu's differentiability theorem
nodes.statement: Let $f : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to ({\mathbb H},d_b)$ be a Lipschitz map. Pansu proved in \cite{Pansu} that for almost every $x \in {\mathbb H}$ there exists a Lipschitz homomorphism $Df(x) : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$ (the Pansu-derivative of $f$ at $x$) so that \[ Df(x) (g) = \lim_{\lambda \to 0} \delta_{1/\lambda} (f(x)^{-1} f(x \delta_\lambda(g))). \]
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz maps of $\mathbb H$ are Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere, with a homomorphism as derivative.
assumptions: Let $f : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to ({\mathbb H},d_b)$ be a Lipschitz map.
conclusions: for almost every $x \in {\mathbb H}$ there exists a Lipschitz homomorphism $Df(x) : {\mathbb H} \to {\mathbb H}$ (the Pansu-derivative of $f$ at $x$)

nodes.name: Magnani's extension of Pansu's theorem to measurable domains
nodes.statement: This result was extended to Lipschitz maps whose domains are measurable subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb H$ by Magnani in \cite{magnani-area}.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
assumptions: Lipschitz maps whose domains are measurable subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb H$
conclusions: This result was extended

nodes.name: Area formula (Magnani)
nodes.statement: \int_{\mathbb H} N(f,A,y) d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(y) = \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x).
nodes.section: 2.1 The Heisenberg group and its distances
nodes.statement_short: Integral of the multiplicity over the image equals the integral of the Jacobian of the Pansu derivative.
conclusions: \int_{\mathbb H} N(f,A,y) d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(y) = \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x).
nodes.label: e:area-formula

nodes.name: Cost function
nodes.statement: Given a metric space $(X,\rho)$, a symmetric function $c:X\times X \to [0,\infty)$ such that $c\leq \rho$ will be called a {\em cost function}.

nodes.name: Set of shortcut pairs S
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\mathcal S}$ all those pairs of points $(x,y)\in X\times X$ such that $c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)$ $${\mathcal S}:=\{ (x,y)\in X\times X\;:\; c(x,y)< \rho(x,y)\}.$$

nodes.name: Shortcut
nodes.statement: An element in ${\mathcal S}$ will be called {\em shortcut} (or flight or tunnel).

nodes.name: Itinerary
nodes.statement: If we have $N\in \mathbb N$ and $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ then the $N$-tuple ${\bf x} = (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ will be called an {\em itinerary} from the extreme points $x_0$ to $x_N$ and we set ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x}):=(x_0,x_N)$ and $\ell({\bf x}) := N$.

nodes.name: Collection of itineraries I
nodes.statement: We will denote by ${\mathcal I}$ the collection of all itineraries in $X$, i.e., $${\mathcal I}:=\{(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \;:\; N\in \mathbb N, \,x_j\in X \}.$$

nodes.name: Cost of an itinerary
nodes.statement: The {\em cost} of an itinerary ${\bf x}= (x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}$ is $$c ({\bf x}):= \sum_{i=1}^N c(x_{i-1}, x_i).$$

nodes.name: Distance associated to a cost function
nodes.statement: The distance $d$ associated to the cost function $c$ is defined as \begin{equation} d(x,y): = \inf\{ c ({\bf x}) \;:\; {\bf x} \in {\mathcal I} ,\, {\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(x,y)\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $d(x,y)$ is the infimum of costs of itineraries from $x$ to $y$.

nodes.name: Shortcut distance (2.5)
nodes.statement: d(x,y): = \inf\{ c ({\bf x}) \;:\; {\bf x} \in {\mathcal I} ,\, {\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(x,y)\}.
nodes.label: eq:ddef

nodes.name: d is a semi-distance, and a distance when dominated below
nodes.statement: It is not too hard to verify symmetry and the triangle inequality for $d$ and so $d$ is a semi-distance on $X$. If there is another distance $d'$ on $X$ such that \[ d'(x,y) \leq c(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] then by the triangle inequality for $d'$, we also have that \[ d'(x,y) \leq d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in X, \] and so $d$ is then a distance.
nodes.statement_short: $d$ is a semi-distance; any distance $d'\le c$ satisfies $d'\le d$, so then $d$ is a distance.
nodes.label: r:d'-leq-c

nodes.name: Alternating itineraries
nodes.statement: We define the subset of {\it alternating itineraries} as $${\mathcal I}_A:=\{{\bf x} \in {\mathcal I} \;:\; (x_{j-1},x_{j})\in {\mathcal S} \iff j \text{ even} \}.$$

nodes.name: Level function
nodes.statement: We shall assign to each shortcut a natural number that we call {\em level} of the shortcut. Namely, a function $L \colon {\mathcal S} \to \mathbb N$ will be called a {\em level function}.

nodes.name: Level function of an alternating itinerary
nodes.statement: We can also define the level function of an alternating itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}_A$ as the function \begin{eqnarray*} L_{\bf x} : \{1,\dots,\lfloor N/2 \rfloor \} &\to& \mathbb N \\ k &\mapsto& L(x_{2k-1},x_{2k}). \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Decreasing-increasing function
nodes.statement: We say that a function $f : \{1,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb R$ is {\em decreasing-increasing} if there is some $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ for which $f|_{[1,k]}$ is decreasing and $f|_{[k+1,n]}$ is increasing (both not necessarily strictly monotonically).
differentia: there is some $k \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ for which $f|_{[1,k]}$ is decreasing and $f|_{[k+1,n]}$ is increasing

nodes.name: Itineraries with decreasing-increasing level functions I*
nodes.statement: We can then define a further subset of itineraries with decreasing-increasing level functions: $${\mathcal I}^*:=\{{\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A \;:\; L_{\bf x} \text{ is decreasing-increasing} \}.$$

nodes.name: Cost ratio sequence alpha_n
nodes.statement: Let $(\alpha_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence of real numbers in $(0,1)$ such that $\alpha_n \downarrow 0$.

nodes.name: Covering constant c_E
nodes.statement: We set $c_E \ge 4$ to be a constant that we now fix.

nodes.name: Net N_n of shortcut centers
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{N}_n := \{x_i\}$ be a set of points in \[ X \setminus \bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1}\bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_j} B_\rho(\{x,y\}, 4\lambda^n) \] such that $\rho(x_i,x_j) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and $X \subseteq \bigcup_i B_\rho(x_i,c_E \lambda^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal N_n$ is a $4\lambda^n$-separated, $c_E\lambda^n$-dense set avoiding neighbourhoods of earlier shortcuts.

nodes.name: Shortcut endpoints q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}
nodes.statement: Using assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} we select for each $i$ points $q_{i,1}, q_{i,2} \in B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n)$ such that \[ \rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} \] and \begin{equation} \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Shortcut property at level n (3.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(p_1, p_2) \le \rho(p_1,q_{i,1}) + \rho(p_2, q_{i,2}) \qquad \text{for all }p_1,p_2 \notin B_\rho(x_i,\lambda^n).
nodes.label: e:general-metric-assumption2

nodes.name: Level n shortcuts, their costs and levels
nodes.statement: Now define the level $n$ shortcuts as \[ {\mathcal S}_n := \{(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2})\,:\, i\} \cup \{(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1})\,:\, i\}, \] their corresponding costs as \[ c(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := c(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := \alpha_n\rho(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) \] and their level as \[ L(q_{i,1}, q_{i,2}) := L(q_{i,2}, q_{i,1}) := n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Level-$n$ shortcuts are the pairs $(q_{i,1},q_{i,2})$ with cost $\alpha_n\rho$ and level $n$.

nodes.name: Total shortcut set S and the distance d
nodes.statement: Finally, let \[ {\mathcal S} := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty {\mathcal S}_n \] and define $d$ as in \eqref{eq:ddef}.

nodes.name: Existence of the nets N_n
nodes.statement: There exists some $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/4)$ depending only on the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$ such that if we set $\lambda \leq \lambda_0$ and $c_E = 8 + \frac1\lambda$, then we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$.
conclusions: There exists some $\lambda_0 \in (0,1/4)$ depending only on the Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$
then we can always find $\mathcal{N}_n$.
nodes.label: lma:constantsexist

nodes.name: Choose lambda small
nodes.statement: Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\rho)$ so that $(X,\rho,\mu)$ is Ahlfors regular (one could use $\mu = \mathcal H^Q$ for instance). We may suppose by taking $\lambda$ small enough (as we are free to do) and using Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho,\mu)$ that \begin{equation} \mu(B_\rho(x,r/4)) - \mu(B_\rho(y,\lambda r)) - \mu(B_\rho(z, \lambda r)) > 0, \qquad \forall x,y,z \in X, 0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix an Ahlfors-regular measure and choose $\lambda$ small so that (3.2) holds.

nodes.name: Small lambda condition (3.2)
nodes.statement: \mu(B_\rho(x,r/4)) - \mu(B_\rho(y,\lambda r)) - \mu(B_\rho(z, \lambda r)) > 0, \qquad \forall x,y,z \in X, 0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X).
nodes.label: e:small-lambda

nodes.name: Earlier shortcut points
nodes.statement: Let $A = \bigcup_{j < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_j} \{x,y\}$. By the definition of $A$, each $x \in A$ comes with a pair $x' \in A$ such that $(x,x') \in S_l$ for some $l < n$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $A$ be the set of earlier shortcut endpoints, paired up.

nodes.name: Claim (3.3)
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{equation} \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}. \end{equation} To see this, taking $y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}$, there exists $y' \in A$ such that $(y,y') \in S_k$ for some $k < n$. Let $x_i^l \in \mathcal{N}_l$ such that $x,x' \in B_\rho(x_i^l,\lambda^l)$ and $x_j^k \in \mathcal{N}_k$ such that $y,y' \in B_\rho(x_j^k,\lambda^k)$. We consider two cases. Suppose first that $k = l$. By the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$ we then have \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,x_j^k) - \rho(x,x_i^l) - \rho(y,x_j^k) \ge 4\lambda^k - \lambda^k - \lambda^k = 2\lambda^k \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \] Suppose now that $k \ne l$. By symmetry we may assume $k < l$. Then by construction, $x_i^l \notin B_\rho(y,4\lambda^l)$ and thus \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,y) - \rho(x,x_i^l) \ge 4\lambda^l - \lambda^l = 3\lambda^l \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \] Thus \eqref{e:A-spread-out} is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Claim (3.3): earlier shortcut points are $2\lambda^{n-1}$-separated from each other except their partners.

nodes.name: State claim
nodes.statement: We claim that \begin{equation} \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: State the separation claim (3.3).

nodes.name: Spread of earlier shortcut points (3.3)
nodes.statement: \rho(x,y) \geq 2 \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad \forall y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}.
nodes.label: e:A-spread-out

nodes.name: Introduce centres
nodes.statement: To see this, taking $y \in A \setminus \{x,x'\}$, there exists $y' \in A$ such that $(y,y') \in S_k$ for some $k < n$. Let $x_i^l \in \mathcal{N}_l$ such that $x,x' \in B_\rho(x_i^l,\lambda^l)$ and $x_j^k \in \mathcal{N}_k$ such that $y,y' \in B_\rho(x_j^k,\lambda^k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a second pair and the net centres of both shortcuts.

nodes.name: Case k = l
nodes.statement: We consider two cases. Suppose first that $k = l$. By the $4\lambda^k$ separation of $\mathcal{N}_k$ we then have \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,x_j^k) - \rho(x,x_i^l) - \rho(y,x_j^k) \ge 4\lambda^k - \lambda^k - \lambda^k = 2\lambda^k \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Same level: use the $4\lambda^k$ separation of the net.

nodes.name: Case k != l
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $k \ne l$. By symmetry we may assume $k < l$. Then by construction, $x_i^l \notin B_\rho(y,4\lambda^l)$ and thus \[ \rho(x,y) \ge \rho(x_i^l,y) - \rho(x,x_i^l) \ge 4\lambda^l - \lambda^l = 3\lambda^l \ge 2\lambda^{n-1}. \] Thus \eqref{e:A-spread-out} is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Different levels: the later centre was chosen away from earlier shortcuts; this proves (3.3).

nodes.name: Maximal net
nodes.statement: Let $\{x_i\}$ be a maximal $4\lambda^n$-separated net of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$. Let $x \in X$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal $4\lambda^n$-separated net of the complement and a point $x$.

nodes.name: Case x near A
nodes.statement: Suppose there exists $y \in A$ such that $\rho(x,y) < 4\lambda^n$. As $\lambda < 1/4$, we get by \eqref{e:A-spread-out} that the number of balls $\{B_\rho(p,4 \lambda^n)\}_{p \in A}$ that intersect $B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1})$ is at most 2. This, together with \eqref{e:small-lambda}, gives that \[ B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n) \neq \emptyset. \]
nodes.statement_short: If $x$ is near $A$, (3.2)-(3.3) give a point near $y$ outside the neighbourhood of $A$.

nodes.name: Covering estimate
nodes.statement: Thus, there exists some $z \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^{n-1}) \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$. As $\{x_i\}$ is also a $4\lambda^n$ covering of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, we get that there exists some $x_i$ such that $\rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n$. Altogether, we get that \[ \rho(x,x_i) \leq \rho(x,y) + \rho(y,z) + \rho(z,x_i) < 4\lambda^n + \lambda^{n-1} + 4 \lambda^n = \left(8 + \frac{1}{\lambda} \right)\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain $x\to y\to z\to x_i$ gives distance $< (8+1/\lambda)\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Case x far from A
nodes.statement: In the case when $x \notin B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$, we are also done as the set $\{x_i\}$ is a $4\lambda^n$-cover of $X \setminus B_\rho(A,4\lambda^n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the net covers $x$ directly.

nodes.name: Removing a level-maximum shortcut does not increase cost
nodes.statement: Suppose ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\mathbb N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$ Then the itinerary ${\bf x}' = (x_0',\dots,x_{N-2}') \in {\mathcal I}_A$ where \[ x_k' = \begin{cases} x_k & k \in \{0,\dots,j+1\}, \\ x_{k+2} & k \in \{j+2,\dots,N-2\}, \end{cases} \] satisfies $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.statement_short: If a middle shortcut has level at least those of its neighbours, removing it gives an itinerary of no greater cost.
assumptions: Suppose ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}_A$ and there exists $j \in 2\mathbb N-1$ such that $$L(x_{j+2},x_{j+3}) \geq \max(L(x_j,x_{j+1}),L(x_{j+4},x_{j+5})).$$
conclusions: satisfies $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ and $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.label: lma:weak-id

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Show the walk endpoints lie outside the shortcut's ball, then apply the shortcut assumption (3.1) to replace the detour by a direct walk.

nodes.name: Subitinerary and claim
nodes.statement: That $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$ is obvious from construction. Consider the subitinerary ${\bf y} = (x_{j+1},x_{j+2},x_{j+3},x_{j+4})$. We claim that $c(x_{j+1},x_{j+4}) \leq c({\bf y})$, which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Endpoints are unchanged; consider the subitinerary ${\bf y}$ and claim the direct walk is no costlier.

nodes.name: Centre of shortcut
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{j+2},x_{j+3})$ was found in $B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$. Then $n= L ( x_{j+2},x_{j+3} )$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $x$ be the net centre of the middle shortcut, of level $n$.

nodes.name: Endpoints outside ball
nodes.statement_short: Inner claim: the walk endpoints lie outside $B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$.

nodes.name: State inner claim
nodes.statement: We claim that $x_{j+1},x_{j+4} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$. Indeed, by assumption, $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: State the inner claim; neighbouring levels are at most $n$.

nodes.name: Case lower level
nodes.statement: So first suppose $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) < n$. Then $x$ was found in the complement of \[ B(x_j,2\lambda^n) \cup B(x_{j+1},2\lambda^n). \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower level: $x$ was chosen away from earlier shortcuts.

nodes.name: Case equal level
nodes.statement: If instead $L(x_j,x_{j+1}) = n$, then let $y \in \mathcal{N}_n$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_j,x_{j+1})$ was found in $B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$. We may assume that $x\neq y$, otherwise $\{x_j,x_{j+1}\}=\{x_{j+2},x_{j+3}\}$ and the claim is obvious. Hence, we have that $\rho(x,y) \geq 4 \lambda^n$ and so \[ B_\rho(x,\lambda^n) \cap B_\rho(y,\lambda^n) = \emptyset. \] As $x_{j+1} \in B_\rho(y,\lambda^n)$, we get that $x_{j+1} \notin B_\rho(x,\lambda^n)$. A similar argument holds for $x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Same level: the two net centres are $4\lambda^n$-separated so the balls are disjoint.

nodes.name: Apply (3.1)
nodes.statement: Thus, we have that the claim follows from \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption2} if we set $x_i=x$, $q_{i,1} = x_{j+2}$, $q_{i,2} = x_{j+3}$, $p_1 = x_{j+1}$, and $p_2 = x_{j+4}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply (3.1) with the shortcut endpoints.

nodes.name: Reduction to decreasing-increasing itineraries with bounded multiplicity
nodes.statement: For any ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A$, there exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$, and \begin{equation} \# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N. \end{equation} Moreover, ${\bf x}$ and ${\bf x}'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Every alternating itinerary can be replaced by one in ${\mathcal I}^*$ of no greater cost using each level at most 4 times.
conclusions: there exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$
${\bf x}$ and ${\bf x}'$ have the same first and last shortcuts.
nodes.label: lma:multiplicity

nodes.name: Level multiplicity bound (3.4)
nodes.statement: \# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N.
nodes.label: e:4-bound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Given an initial ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A$, we iterate Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} until we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ for which there are no indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. As the length of the itinerary shrinks by 2 with each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, we get that we have to stop after some finite number of iterations. It is elementary to see that if $L_{\bf x'} : \{0,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb N$ satisfies $$L_{{\bf x}'}(i+1) < \max (L_{{\bf x}'}(i),L_{{\bf x}'}(i+2)), \qquad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,n-2\},$$ then $L_{{\bf x}'}$ is decreasing-increasing, which means that ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$. Now suppose $\# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) > 4$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$. As ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we get that there exists some $i \in 2\mathbb N$ so that $$L(x_i,x_{i+1}) = L(x_{i+2},x_{i+3}) = L(x_{i+4},x_{i+5}).$$ But this contradicts the assumption that ${\bf x}'$ does not have any indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. Finally, since each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} keeps the first and last shortcut of ${\bf x}$ unchanged the resulting itinerary ${\bf x}'$ has the same first and last shortcut as ${\bf x}$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Lemma 3.2 until no index qualifies; the result is decreasing-increasing and repeats no level more than 4 times.

nodes.name: Iterate Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement: Given an initial ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}_A$, we iterate Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} until we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ for which there are no indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}. As the length of the itinerary shrinks by 2 with each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, we get that we have to stop after some finite number of iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Lemma 3.2; the length drops by 2 each time so it terminates.

nodes.name: Decreasing-increasing
nodes.statement: It is elementary to see that if $L_{\bf x'} : \{0,\dots,n\} \to \mathbb N$ satisfies $$L_{{\bf x}'}(i+1) < \max (L_{{\bf x}'}(i),L_{{\bf x}'}(i+2)), \qquad \forall i \in \{0,\dots,n-2\},$$ then $L_{{\bf x}'}$ is decreasing-increasing, which means that ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: No qualifying index means the level function is decreasing-increasing.

nodes.name: Multiplicity bound
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\# L_{{\bf x}'}^{-1}(k) > 4$ for some $k \in \mathbb N$. As ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we get that there exists some $i \in 2\mathbb N$ so that $$L(x_i,x_{i+1}) = L(x_{i+2},x_{i+3}) = L(x_{i+4},x_{i+5}).$$ But this contradicts the assumption that ${\bf x}'$ does not have any indices that satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}.
nodes.statement_short: More than 4 equal levels would give three consecutive equal levels, contradicting termination.

nodes.name: Endpoints shortcuts kept
nodes.statement: Finally, since each application of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id} keeps the first and last shortcut of ${\bf x}$ unchanged the resulting itinerary ${\bf x}'$ has the same first and last shortcut as ${\bf x}$.
nodes.statement_short: First and last shortcuts are preserved.

nodes.name: d is a distance
nodes.statement: The function $d$ is a distance on $X$.
conclusions: The function $d$ is a distance on $X$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: The validity of the triangle inequality follows from the definition of the distance as defined in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Symmetry is due to the symmetry of the cost function. What needs to be checked is that $x \ne y$ implies $d(x,y)>0$. In order to show this, suppose that $x,y \in X$ with $\rho(x,y)>0$. Let $n \in \mathbb N$ be such that \[ 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \le \frac12\rho(x,y). \] Let $(\alpha_n)$ be the sequence of positive numbers used to construct the cost function in Section~\ref{sec:construction}. Consider the positive number \[ \varepsilon := \min\left(\frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1}, \frac14\rho(x,y)\right). \] Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq d(x,y) + \varepsilon$, and $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} (remember that using stationary walks every itinerary can be modified to be an alternating itinerary of no greater cost, because of triangle inequality). On the one hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) = \emptyset$, then the alternating itinerary does not have shortcuts at odd steps and it has them at even steps only of level greater that $n$ and with multiplicity at most $4$. Hence, we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(x,y) & \ge & c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge \sum_{j \text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \varepsilon \ge \rho(x,y) - \sum_{j \text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \frac14\rho(x,y)\\ & \ge & \frac34\rho(x,y) - 4 \sum_{k=n}^\infty 2\lambda^k \ge \frac34\rho(x,y) - 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \ge \frac14\rho(x,y) > 0, \end{eqnarray*} where we used that a point in a shortcuts at level $k$ has $\rho$-distance less than $ \lambda^k$ from the center of the ball in which the shortcut was found. On the other hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) \ne \emptyset$, then, if $(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell)$ is a shortcut at level $l<n$ of ${\bf x}$, we have \[ d(x,y) \ge c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) - \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} \ge \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0, \] where we used that $ c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) = \alpha_l \rho(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) \geq \alpha_l \lambda^l.$ In both cases $d(x,y) > 0$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Positivity via a near-optimal itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$: either all shortcuts are of high level (geometric tail bound) or a low-level shortcut has cost bounded below.

nodes.name: Reduce to positivity
nodes.statement: The validity of the triangle inequality follows from the definition of the distance as defined in \eqref{eq:ddef}. Symmetry is due to the symmetry of the cost function. What needs to be checked is that $x \ne y$ implies $d(x,y)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality and symmetry are immediate; positivity remains.

nodes.name: Choose n and epsilon
nodes.statement: In order to show this, suppose that $x,y \in X$ with $\rho(x,y)>0$. Let $n \in \mathbb N$ be such that \[ 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \le \frac12\rho(x,y). \] Let $(\alpha_n)$ be the sequence of positive numbers used to construct the cost function in Section~\ref{sec:construction}. Consider the positive number \[ \varepsilon := \min\left(\frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1}, \frac14\rho(x,y)\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose $n$ with $8\lambda^n/(1-\lambda)\le\rho(x,y)/2$ and a small $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Near-optimal itinerary
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq d(x,y) + \varepsilon$, and $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$, which exists by Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} (remember that using stationary walks every itinerary can be modified to be an alternating itinerary of no greater cost, because of triangle inequality).
nodes.statement_short: Take a near-optimal itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$ with multiplicity at most 4 by Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: Case only high levels
nodes.statement: On the one hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) = \emptyset$, then the alternating itinerary does not have shortcuts at odd steps and it has them at even steps only of level greater that $n$ and with multiplicity at most $4$. Hence, we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(x,y) & \ge & c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge \sum_{j \text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \varepsilon \ge \rho(x,y) - \sum_{j \text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) - \frac14\rho(x,y)\\ & \ge & \frac34\rho(x,y) - 4 \sum_{k=n}^\infty 2\lambda^k \ge \frac34\rho(x,y) - 8 \frac{\lambda^{n}}{1-\lambda} \ge \frac14\rho(x,y) > 0, \end{eqnarray*} where we used that a point in a shortcuts at level $k$ has $\rho$-distance less than $ \lambda^k$ from the center of the ball in which the shortcut was found.
nodes.statement_short: No low-level shortcuts: the shortcut lengths sum to a small geometric tail.

nodes.name: Case a low level
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([1,n-1]) \ne \emptyset$, then, if $(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell)$ is a shortcut at level $l<n$ of ${\bf x}$, we have \[ d(x,y) \ge c({\bf x}) - \varepsilon \ge c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) - \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} \ge \frac12\min_{k \in [1,n-1]} \alpha_k\lambda^{k+1} > 0, \] where we used that $ c(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) = \alpha_l \rho(x_{\ell-1},x_\ell) \geq \alpha_l \lambda^l.$
nodes.statement_short: A low-level shortcut costs at least $\alpha_l\lambda^l$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In both cases $d(x,y) > 0$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $d(x,y)>0$.

nodes.name: At most one low-level shortcut meets a small d-ball
nodes.statement: Let $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \lambda^n$. There exists at most one pair $\{q_1,q_2\}$ such that $(q_1,q_2) \in {\mathcal S}$, $L(q_1,q_2) < n$ and $\{q_1,q_2\} \cap B_d(x,r) \ne \emptyset$.
conclusions: There exists at most one pair $\{q_1,q_2\}$ such that $(q_1,q_2) \in {\mathcal S}$, $L(q_1,q_2) < n$ and $\{q_1,q_2\} \cap B_d(x,r) \ne \emptyset$.
nodes.label: lma:largegaps

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: Suppose to the contrary that there exist two disjoint $(q_1,q_2), (\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ with \begin{equation} L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n \end{equation} and $q_1,\tilde q_1 \in B_d(x,r)$. Then \[ d(q_1,\tilde q_1) \le d(q_1,x) + d(x,\tilde q_1) < 2r \le 2\lambda^n. \] Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $x_0=q_1,$ $x_N=\tilde q_1$ and \begin{equation} c({\bf x}) < 2\lambda^n. \end{equation} We may assume that $N$ is odd, up to adding a stationary walk at the end. Hence the slightly longer itinerary ${\bf y}=(q_2,q_2,q_1,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2)$ is an alternating itinerary. By applying Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} to ${\bf y}$ we know that there exists $ {\bf y}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $ c( {\bf y}') \le c( {\bf y}), $ where $ {\rm Ext}( {\bf y}') ={\rm Ext} ( {\bf y}) $. Notice that, since the construction in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} keeps the the first and last shortcuts stay the same, we have that ${\bf y}'$ is of the form \[{\bf y}' = (q_2,q_2,q_1,x'_1,\dots,x'_{N'}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) .\] We conclude that the itinerary ${\bf x}$ may be replaced with no extra cost by an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ that is decreasing-increasing and, due to \eqref{e:shortcut-lower-bnds}, we have $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([n,\infty]) = \emptyset$. We remark that the itinerary ${\bf x}'$ cannot have only stationary walks, i.e., there is some $j \in 2\mathbb Z$ so that $x'_j \neq x'_{j+1}$. Indeed, otherwise the itinerary cannot move away from $\{q_1,q_2\}$, since distinct shortcuts are separated. Hence, there are two distinct shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Set $k_1:= L(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$ $k_2:= L(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Recall that $k_1,k_2<n$. Let $a, b$ are the centers of the balls in which the shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$ were found with radii $\lambda^{k_1}$ and $\lambda^{k_2}$, respectively. Let us distinguish two cases. Assume first that $k_1=k_2=:k$, so that $a$ and $ b$ are $4\lambda^{k}$ separated. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(a,b) -\rho(a,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k} - \lambda^{k}- \lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^n. \] Suppose now $k_1\neq k_2$, say that $k_1< k_2$, the other case is similar. Recall that $b$ was found outside $B(x'_j,4\lambda^{k_2})$ in the construction of the shortcuts. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(b,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k_2} - \lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^n. \] In either case we have \[ c({\bf x}) \ge c({\bf x}') \ge \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge 2\lambda^n, \] which is in contradiction with \eqref{eq:q1q1small}.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: a cheap itinerary joining two low-level shortcuts must walk between separated shortcuts, costing at least $2\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Assume two shortcuts
nodes.statement: Suppose to the contrary that there exist two disjoint $(q_1,q_2), (\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ with \begin{equation} L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n \end{equation} and $q_1,\tilde q_1 \in B_d(x,r)$. Then \[ d(q_1,\tilde q_1) \le d(q_1,x) + d(x,\tilde q_1) < 2r \le 2\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume two low-level shortcuts meet the ball; their endpoints are $d$-close.

nodes.name: Low levels of two shortcuts (3.5)
nodes.statement: L(q_1,q_2), L(\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) < n
nodes.label: e:shortcut-lower-bnds

nodes.name: Cheap itinerary
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $x_0=q_1,$ $x_N=\tilde q_1$ and \begin{equation} c({\bf x}) < 2\lambda^n. \end{equation} We may assume that $N$ is odd, up to adding a stationary walk at the end.
nodes.statement_short: Take a cheap itinerary between them, of odd length.

nodes.name: Small cost itinerary (3.6)
nodes.statement: c({\bf x}) < 2\lambda^n.
nodes.label: eq:q1q1small

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Hence the slightly longer itinerary ${\bf y}=(q_2,q_2,q_1,x_1,\dots,x_{N-1}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2)$ is an alternating itinerary. By applying Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} to ${\bf y}$ we know that there exists $ {\bf y}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $ c( {\bf y}') \le c( {\bf y}), $ where $ {\rm Ext}( {\bf y}') ={\rm Ext} ( {\bf y}) $.
nodes.statement_short: Extend by the two shortcuts and apply Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: Only low levels
nodes.statement: Notice that, since the construction in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} keeps the the first and last shortcuts stay the same, we have that ${\bf y}'$ is of the form \[{\bf y}' = (q_2,q_2,q_1,x'_1,\dots,x'_{N'}, \tilde q_1,\tilde q_2) .\] We conclude that the itinerary ${\bf x}$ may be replaced with no extra cost by an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ that is decreasing-increasing and, due to \eqref{e:shortcut-lower-bnds}, we have $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([n,\infty]) = \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: The reduced itinerary keeps the end shortcuts and uses only levels below $n$.

nodes.name: Non-stationary walk
nodes.statement: We remark that the itinerary ${\bf x}'$ cannot have only stationary walks, i.e., there is some $j \in 2\mathbb Z$ so that $x'_j \neq x'_{j+1}$. Indeed, otherwise the itinerary cannot move away from $\{q_1,q_2\}$, since distinct shortcuts are separated.
nodes.statement_short: The itinerary must contain a genuine walk.

nodes.name: Two shortcuts
nodes.statement: Hence, there are two distinct shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Set $k_1:= L(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$ $k_2:= L(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$. Recall that $k_1,k_2<n$. Let $a, b$ are the centers of the balls in which the shortcuts $(x'_{j-1},x'_j)$, $(x'_{j+1},x'_{j+2})$ were found with radii $\lambda^{k_1}$ and $\lambda^{k_2}$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Name two consecutive shortcuts, their levels and centres.

nodes.name: Case equal levels
nodes.statement: Let us distinguish two cases. Assume first that $k_1=k_2=:k$, so that $a$ and $ b$ are $4\lambda^{k}$ separated. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(a,b) -\rho(a,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k} - \lambda^{k}- \lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^{k} \ge 2\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equal levels: separation of centres gives a walk of length $\ge 2\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Case different levels
nodes.statement: Suppose now $k_1\neq k_2$, say that $k_1< k_2$, the other case is similar. Recall that $b$ was found outside $B(x'_j,4\lambda^{k_2})$ in the construction of the shortcuts. Hence, we have \[ \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge \rho(b,x'_j) -\rho(b,x'_{j+1}) \ge 4 \lambda^{k_2} - \lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^{k_2} \ge 3\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Different levels: the later centre was chosen far from earlier shortcuts.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: In either case we have \[ c({\bf x}) \ge c({\bf x}') \ge \rho(x'_j,x'_{j+1}) \ge 2\lambda^n, \] which is in contradiction with \eqref{eq:q1q1small}.
nodes.statement_short: The cost is at least $2\lambda^n$, contradicting (3.6).

nodes.name: Ball inclusions between d and rho
nodes.statement: For all $x \in X$ and $r > 0$ there exist $y_1,y_2 \in X$ such that \begin{equation} B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A $d$-ball contains the $\rho$-ball of the same radius and lies in comparable $\rho$-balls around two points.
conclusions: there exist $y_1,y_2 \in X$ such that \begin{equation} B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)  \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right). \end{equation}
nodes.label: lma:inclusions

nodes.name: Ball inclusions (3.7)
nodes.statement: B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r) \subseteq B_\rho\left(\{y_1,y_2\},\left(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2)\right)r\right).
nodes.label: eq:inclusions

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$. Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})=(x,z)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$. Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \mathbb N \cup\{0\}$ be such that \[ \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n. \] By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ and \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset. \end{equation} If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$. Now \[ B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r). \] Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even. Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = n}^\infty \lambda^k = 2r + 8\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $ \lambda^{n+1} \le r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on $r\ge1$ or $r<1$; Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 bound the walking part of near-optimal itineraries by a geometric series.

nodes.name: First inclusion
nodes.statement: The first inclusion $B_\rho(x,r) \subseteq B_d(x,r)$ follows from the fact that by construction $d \le \rho$.
nodes.statement_short: First inclusion from $d\le\rho$.

nodes.name: Large radius
nodes.statement: Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})=(x,z)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$.
nodes.statement_short: Second inclusion for $r\ge1$.

nodes.name: Case r >= 1
nodes.statement: Let us show the second inclusion. Suppose first that $r \ge 1$. Let $z \in B_d(x,r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $r\ge1$; take $z$ in the $d$-ball.

nodes.name: Bound rho(x,z)
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})=(x,z)$, $c({\bf x}) \leq r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Then \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(x,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = 1}^\infty \lambda^k \leq r + 8\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $\lambda <1<r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds with $y_1=y_2=x$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.3 itinerary: walking cost plus geometric sum of shortcut lengths.

nodes.name: Case r < 1
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $r < 1$ and let $n \in \mathbb N \cup\{0\}$ be such that \[ \lambda^{n+1} \le r < \lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Case $r<1$; choose $n$ with $\lambda^{n+1}\le r<\lambda^n$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.5
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lma:largegaps} there exists at most one pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ such that $(y_1,y_2) \in {\mathcal S}$ and \begin{equation} L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset. \end{equation} If such pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ does not exist, we define $y_1 = y_2 = x$. Now \[ B_d(x,r) \subset B_d(\{y_1,y_2\},2r). \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.5 gives at most one low-level shortcut pair $\{y_1,y_2\}$ near $x$.

nodes.name: Only one big jump (3.8)
nodes.statement: L(y_1,y_2) < n \quad\text{and}\qquad B_d(x,r) \cap \{y_1,y_2\} \ne \emptyset.
nodes.label: eq:onlyonebigjump

nodes.name: Itinerary from y_1
nodes.statement: Take $z \in B_d(x,r)$. By symmetry we may suppose $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} there exists ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with ${\rm Ext} ({\bf x})=(y_1,z)$, $c({\bf x}) < 2r$, and $\# L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) < 4$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. By the assumption $d(z,y_1) \le d(z,y_2)$ we may assume that ${\bf x}$ does not contain the shortcuts $(y_1,y_2),(y_2,y_1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:onlyonebigjump} we have $L(x_{j-1},x_j) \ge n$ for all $j$ even.
nodes.statement_short: Take an itinerary from $y_1$ to $z$ avoiding that shortcut; all its shortcuts have level $\ge n$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Then, by the fact that ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(y_1,z) & \le & \sum_{j=1}^N\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) \le \sum_{j\text{ odd}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j) + \sum_{j\text{ even}}\rho(x_{j-1},x_j)\\ & \le & c({\bf x}) + 8\sum_{k = n}^\infty \lambda^k = 2r + 8\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda} \le \left(2 + 8\frac{\lambda^{-1}}{1-\lambda} \right)r, \end{eqnarray*} since $ \lambda^{n+1} \le r$, and hence \eqref{eq:inclusions} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Geometric tail bound gives (3.7).

nodes.name: Proof of Ahlfors Q-regularity of (X,d)
nodes.statement: We now give the proof of the Ahlfors $Q$-regularity of the space $(X,d)$, assuming that $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular. Namely, we have that there exists a constant $C < \infty$ such that \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_\rho(x,r)) \le Cr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}_\rho(X)$. Hence by Lemma~\ref{lma:inclusions} we have \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_d(x,r)) \le C2(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))^Qr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < (2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))r < \operatorname{diam}_\rho(X)$. Thus $(X,d)$ is also Ahlfors $Q$-regular.
nodes.statement_short: Ahlfors regularity of $\rho$ plus the ball inclusions of Lemma 3.6.

nodes.name: Recall regularity
nodes.statement: We now give the proof of the Ahlfors $Q$-regularity of the space $(X,d)$, assuming that $(X,\rho)$ is Ahlfors $Q$-regular. Namely, we have that there exists a constant $C < \infty$ such that \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_\rho(x,r)) \le Cr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}_\rho(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall Ahlfors regularity of $(X,\rho)$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Hence by Lemma~\ref{lma:inclusions} we have \[ \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q_\rho(B_d(x,r)) \le C2(2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))^Qr^Q, \] for all $x \in X$ and $0 < (2 + 8/(\lambda -\lambda^2))r < \operatorname{diam}_\rho(X)$. Thus $(X,d)$ is also Ahlfors $Q$-regular.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.6 transfers the measure bounds to $d$-balls.

nodes.name: Proof that d and rho are not biLipschitz on positive-measure sets
nodes.statement: Let $A\subseteq X$ be such that $\mathcal H^4_{\rho}(A)>0$. Our aim is to show that $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$. For this purpose take a density-point $x$ of $A$. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $r_\epsilon > 0$ such that \[ B_\rho(x,r) \subset B_\rho(A,\epsilon r), \qquad \text{for all }r \in (0,r_\epsilon). \] Now, for all $n \in \mathbb N$ there exists $(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) \in {\mathcal S}$ with $L(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) = n$ such that \[ \{q_{n,1},q_{n,2}\} \subset B_\rho(x,2c_E\lambda^n). \] If $3c_E\lambda^n < r_\epsilon$, there exist $x_{n,1},x_{n,2} \in A$ such that \[ \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \qquad \text{and}\qquad \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n. \] Then \[ \rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) \ge \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) - \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) - \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \] and \begin{eqnarray*} d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) & \le & d(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + d(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + d(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & \alpha_n \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & 2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore we have \[ \frac{d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})}{\rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})} \le \frac{2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n}{\lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n} = \frac{2\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon}{\lambda-6c_E\epsilon}. \] As $\alpha_n \to 0$, by letting $n$ be sufficiently large and $\epsilon$ be sufficiently small, we get that $\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon$ is sufficently small and so the distances $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.statement_short: At a density point of $A$, approximate the endpoints of level-$n$ shortcuts by points of $A$; their $d/\rho$ ratio tends to $0$ as $\alpha_n\to0$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let $A\subseteq X$ be such that $\mathcal H^4_{\rho}(A)>0$. Our aim is to show that $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: no biLipschitz equivalence on $A$.

nodes.name: Density point
nodes.statement: For this purpose take a density-point $x$ of $A$. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists $r_\epsilon > 0$ such that \[ B_\rho(x,r) \subset B_\rho(A,\epsilon r), \qquad \text{for all }r \in (0,r_\epsilon). \]
nodes.statement_short: Take a density point $x$ of $A$.

nodes.name: Nearby shortcut
nodes.statement: Now, for all $n \in \mathbb N$ there exists $(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) \in {\mathcal S}$ with $L(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) = n$ such that \[ \{q_{n,1},q_{n,2}\} \subset B_\rho(x,2c_E\lambda^n). \]
nodes.statement_short: A level-$n$ shortcut lies near $x$ by the covering property.

nodes.name: Points of A
nodes.statement: If $3c_E\lambda^n < r_\epsilon$, there exist $x_{n,1},x_{n,2} \in A$ such that \[ \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \qquad \text{and}\qquad \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \le 3c_E\epsilon\lambda^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the shortcut endpoints by points of $A$.

nodes.name: Estimates
nodes.statement: Then \[ \rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) \ge \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) - \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) - \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2}) \ge \lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n \] and \begin{eqnarray*} d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2}) & \le & d(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + d(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + d(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & \alpha_n \rho(q_{n,1},q_{n,2}) + \rho(x_{n,1},q_{n,1}) + \rho(x_{n,2},q_{n,2})\\ & \le & 2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound for $\rho$ and upper bound for $d$ between these points.

nodes.name: Ratio bound
nodes.statement: Therefore we have \[ \frac{d(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})}{\rho(x_{n,1},x_{n,2})} \le \frac{2\alpha_n\lambda^n + 6c_E\epsilon \lambda^n}{\lambda^{n+1} - 6c_E\epsilon\lambda^n} = \frac{2\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon}{\lambda-6c_E\epsilon}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Ratio $d/\rho$ bounded by $(2\alpha_n+6c_E\epsilon)/(\lambda-6c_E\epsilon)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: As $\alpha_n \to 0$, by letting $n$ be sufficiently large and $\epsilon$ be sufficiently small, we get that $\alpha_n + 6c_E\epsilon$ is sufficently small and so the distances $d$ and $\rho$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\alpha_n\to0$ the ratio can be made arbitrarily small.

nodes.name: Zero-cost shortcuts are allowed
nodes.statement: In the definition of the costs for the shortcuts we could also allow $\alpha_n = 0$. This would give a semi-distance on $X$ that, upon factoring, gives a metric space $(Y,d)$ that satisfies all the previous properties.
nodes.statement_short: Allowing $\alpha_n=0$ gives a semi-distance whose quotient still has all the properties.
nodes.label: rmk:zerocost

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: We will verify that the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold in the Heisenberg group with $\lambda = \frac12$. Let $p \in \mathbb H$ and $r > 0$. By left-translation invariance of the distance $d_b$ in $\mathbb H$ we may assume that $p = (0,0,0)$. Take $q_1 = (0,0,0)$ and $q_2 = (0,0,r^2/4)$. Now let $p_1,p_2 \notin B(0,r)$. Since $d_b(q_1,q_2) = \sqrt{r^2/4} = r/2$, by the triangle inequality we have that $d_b(p_1,q_1) \ge r/2$ and $d_b(p_2,q_2) \ge r/2$. Write $p_1 = (x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $p_2 = (x_2,y_2,z_2)$. Then the equation for the box distance is given by \eqref{eq:box:dist}. Trivially, we have \[ |x_1-x_2| \le |x_1| + |x_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2) \] and \[ |y_2-y_1| \le |y_1| + |y_2| \le d_b(p_1,q_1) + d_b(p_2,q_2). \] By using the triangle inequality and the estimate $r^2/4 \le d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)$ we also get \begin{eqnarray*} \left|z_1-z_2-\frac12(x_1y_2-x_2y_1) \right| & \le & |z_1|+|z_2-\frac14r^2|+\frac14r^2 +\frac12|x_1||y_2| + \frac12|x_2||y_1|\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2+d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & & +\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+2d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2\\ & = & \left(d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2)\right)^2. \end{eqnarray*} Thus we have \[ d_b(p_1,p_2) \le d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2) \] as required by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the shortcut assumption of Theorem 1.3 for the box distance with $\lambda=1/2$, using vertical shortcuts $q_1=0$, $q_2=(0,0,r^2/4)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to origin
nodes.statement: We will verify that the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold in the Heisenberg group with $\lambda = \frac12$. Let $p \in \mathbb H$ and $r > 0$. By left-translation invariance of the distance $d_b$ in $\mathbb H$ we may assume that $p = (0,0,0)$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify Theorem 1.3's assumptions with $\lambda=1/2$; by left-invariance take $p=0$.

nodes.name: Choose shortcut
nodes.statement: Take $q_1 = (0,0,0)$ and $q_2 = (0,0,r^2/4)$. Now let $p_1,p_2 \notin B(0,r)$. Since $d_b(q_1,q_2) = \sqrt{r^2/4} = r/2$, by the triangle inequality we have that $d_b(p_1,q_1) \ge r/2$ and $d_b(p_2,q_2) \ge r/2$. Write $p_1 = (x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $p_2 = (x_2,y_2,z_2)$. Then the equation for the box distance is given by \eqref{eq:box:dist}.
nodes.statement_short: Vertical shortcut $q_1=0$, $q_2=(0,0,r^2/4)$; points outside the ball are at distance $\ge r/2$.

nodes.name: Horizontal components
nodes.statement_short: Horizontal components are bounded trivially.

nodes.name: Vertical component
nodes.statement: By using the triangle inequality and the estimate $r^2/4 \le d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)$ we also get \begin{eqnarray*} \left|z_1-z_2-\frac12(x_1y_2-x_2y_1) \right| & \le & |z_1|+|z_2-\frac14r^2|+\frac14r^2 +\frac12|x_1||y_2| + \frac12|x_2||y_1|\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2+d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & & +\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+\frac12d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)\\ & \le & d_b(p_1,q_1)^2+2d_b(q_1,p_1)d_b(q_2,p_2)+d_b(p_2,q_2)^2\\ & = & \left(d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2)\right)^2. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Vertical component bounded by $(d_b(q_1,p_1)+d_b(q_2,p_2))^2$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus we have \[ d_b(p_1,p_2) \le d_b(q_1,p_1) + d_b(q_2,p_2) \] as required by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude (1.1).

nodes.name: Snowflaked Ahlfors-regular spaces admit shortcuts
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be an Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space with $Q > 0$ and let $\delta \in (0,1)$. Then the snowflaked metric space $(X,d^\delta)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Consequently, there exists a distance $d'$ on $X$ such that $d' \le d^\delta$, $(X,d')$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular, and for any $A\subseteq X$ with $\mathcal H^{Q/\delta}_{d^\delta}(A)>0$, we have that $d'$ and $d^\delta$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Shortcuts in snowflaked Ahlfors regular metric spaces
nodes.statement_short: Snowflakes $(X,d^\delta)$ of Ahlfors-regular spaces satisfy Theorem 1.3, giving a non-biLipschitz Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular distance.
assumptions: Let $(X,d)$ be an Ahlfors $Q$-regular metric space with $Q > 0$ and let $\delta \in (0,1)$.
conclusions: the snowflaked metric space $(X,d^\delta)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}.

there exists a distance $d'$ on $X$ such that $d' \le d^\delta$, $(X,d')$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular, and for any $A\subseteq X$ with $\mathcal H^{Q/\delta}_{d^\delta}(A)>0$, we have that $d'$ and $d^\delta$ are not biLipschitz equivalent on $A$.
nodes.label: thm:Ahlforssnowflake

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: First of all, it is trivial that $(X,d^\delta)$ is Ahlfors $Q/\delta$-regular. Let us then check the assumption (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:general}. Since $(X,d)$ is $Q$-regular, there exists $C > 1$ such that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{C}r^Q \le \mathcal{H}^Q(B_d(x,r)) \le Cr^Q \end{equation} for all $x \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$. We shall set $\lambda:= (2C)^{-2\delta/Q}(1-\delta)^\delta$. Take $p \in X$ and $0 < r < \operatorname{diam}(X)$. Define $q_1 = p$ and take \[ q_2 \in B_d(p,(1-\delta)r^\frac{1}{\delta}) \setminus B_d(p, (2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta) r^\frac{1}{\delta}). \] Such $q_2$ exists since the annulus from where the point is taken has positive measure by \eqref{eq:ahlfors} and is hence non-empty. In particular, $q_1, q_2\in B_{d^\delta} (p,r)$ and \[ d(q_1,q_2)^\delta \ge \left((2C)^{-2/Q}(1-\delta)\right)^\delta r = \lambda r. \] Now, take $p_1,p_2 \notin B_d\left(p,r^\frac{1}{\delta}\right)$. We get that $$ d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2) \geq \delta r^{1/\delta},$$ and so $$d(q_1,q_2) \leq \left( 1 - \delta\right) r^{1/\delta} \leq \left( \frac{1}{\delta} - 1 \right) \min(d(q_1,p_1),d(q_2,p_2)).$$ First assume that $d(p_1,q_1) \le d(p_2,q_2)$. Then we get \begin{eqnarray*} d(p_1,p_2)^\delta & \le & (d(p_1,q_1)+d(q_1,q_2)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta \\ & \le & ((1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)+d(p_2,q_2))^\delta\\ & \le & d(p_2,q_2)^\delta + \delta(1+(\frac1\delta-1))d(p_1,q_1)d(p_2,q_2)^{1-\delta} \\ & \le & d(p_1,q_1)^\delta + d(p_2,q_2)^\delta \end{eqnarray*} verifying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption}. In the penultimate inequality, we used the fact that $x \mapsto x^\delta$ is concave so that the higher order terms of the Taylor expansion is always negative. An analogous calculation takes care of the case $d(p_2,q_2) \leq d(p_1,q_1)$.

nodes.statement_short: Pick $q_2$ in an annulus (nonempty by Ahlfors regularity) and verify (1.1) by concavity of $x\mapsto x^\delta$.

nodes.name: Similitudes S_{i,j,k}
nodes.statement: Define the similitude mappings as \[ S_{i,j,k}(p) = \left(\frac{i}{2},\frac{j}{2},\frac{k}{4}\right) \cdot \delta_\frac12(p), \qquad i,j \in \{0,1\}, k \in \{0,1,2,3\}. \]

nodes.name: Self-similar set K (attractor)
nodes.statement: Relabel the similitudes by $\{S_i\,:\,i = 1,\dots,16\} = \{S_{i,j,k}\}$ and denote by $K$ the attractor of $\{S_{i,j,k}\}$, i.e., the nonempty compact set (see \cite{Hutchinson} for details) satisfying \begin{equation} K = \bigcup_{i=1}^{16}S_i(K). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Self-similarity of K (5.1)
nodes.statement: K = \bigcup_{i=1}^{16}S_i(K).
nodes.label: e:K-self-similar

nodes.name: Proof that K has nonempty interior
nodes.statement: First of all, the horizontal projection of the iterated function system has the unit square as the attractor. Secondly, since the dilation and the group operation commute, we may consider separately the horizontal and vertical components of the iterated function system. This way we see that \begin{equation} K = \{(x,y,z+t) \,:\, (x,y,z) \in \widetilde K, t \in [0,1]\}, \end{equation} where $\widetilde K$ is the attractor of the horizontal component that is realized as the attractor of the system \[ \{S_{i,j,0}\,:\, i,j \in \{0,1\}\}. \] The set $\widetilde K$ has the form \begin{equation} \widetilde K = \overline{\{(x,y,\varphi(x,y))\,:\,(x,y)\in [0,1]^2\}} \end{equation} with some Borel function $\varphi \colon [0,1]^2 \to \mathbb R$. Observe that $\varphi$ is bounded since $K$ is compact. Also, since $0$ is the fixed point of $S_{0,0,0}$ and $S_{i,j,0}(\widetilde K)$ do not contain $0$ if $i\ne 0$ or $j \ne 0$, the function $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the IFS into horizontal and vertical parts: $K$ is a vertical unit thickening of a graph that is continuous at $0$.

nodes.name: Decompose IFS
nodes.statement: First of all, the horizontal projection of the iterated function system has the unit square as the attractor. This way we see that \begin{equation} K = \{(x,y,z+t) \,:\, (x,y,z) \in \widetilde K, t \in [0,1]\}, \end{equation} where $\widetilde K$ is the attractor of the horizontal component that is realized as the attractor of the system \[ \{S_{i,j,0}\,:\, i,j \in \{0,1\}\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Separate horizontal and vertical components: $K$ is a vertical unit thickening of $\widetilde K$.
