nodes.name: Composition S_i along a multi-index
nodes.statement: For a multi-index $\mathtt{i}= (i_1,...,i_k) \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, we shall use the standard notation $S_{\mathtt{i}}$ for the composition \[ S_{\mathtt{i}}:= S_{i_1} \circ S_{i_2} \circ \cdots \circ S_{i_k}.\] With $k=0$ we interpret $\{1,\dots,16\}^k$ to consist of only one element, call it $\emptyset$, and $S_\emptyset$ is then understood to be the identity map.

nodes.name: Self-similar level n shortcuts in K
nodes.statement: We define the shortcuts at level $n$ as \[ {\mathcal S}_n := \{(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,\frac1{64}))\,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\}. \]

nodes.name: Levels of the self-similar shortcuts
nodes.statement: We also set $L(x,y) = n$ for $(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_n$. Note that levels start from $n = 3$.

nodes.name: Total self-similar shortcut set
nodes.statement: We then define the total set of shortcuts as \[ {\mathcal S} := \bigcup_{n=3}^\infty {\mathcal S}_n. \]

nodes.name: Zero cost of self-similar shortcuts
nodes.statement: Define the cost as $c(x,y) = 0$ for all $(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}$.

nodes.name: Horizontal projection pi
nodes.statement: In the following lemmas we will use the map \[\pi : ({\mathbb H},d_b) \to \mathbb R^2\] that is the projection onto the $xy$-plane and is a $1$-Lipschitz homomorphism, when we endow $\mathbb R^2$ with the $\ell_\infty$-distance.

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centers avoid neighbourhoods of lower-level shortcuts
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$, we have \[ \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \cap \left( \bigcup_{m < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_m} B_{d_b}(\{x,y\},2^{-n+2}) \right) = \emptyset. \]
conclusions: \[ \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \cap \left( \bigcup_{m < n} \bigcup_{(x,y) \in {\mathcal S}_m} B_{d_b}(\{x,y\},2^{-n+2}) \right) = \emptyset. \]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$. Note that for each $k$ we have that \[ \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \mathbb R\}) = A_k. \] As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that \[ A_n \cap B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset. \] But this follows from the geometry of $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Note that we need the sets $B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.
nodes.statement_short: Project to the plane by the 1-Lipschitz map $\pi$, where shortcut centers are centers of dyadic squares.

nodes.name: Dyadic centres
nodes.statement: Let $A_k \subset [0,1]^2$ be the centers of the dyadic subcubes of level $k$. Note that for each $k$ we have that \[ \pi(\{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,t) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k, t \in \mathbb R\}) = A_k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Shortcut centres project to dyadic centres $A_k$.

nodes.name: Reduce to plane
nodes.statement: As $\pi$ is 1-Lipschitz, it suffices to prove that \[ A_n \cap B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty} \left( \bigcup_{m < n} A_m, 2^{-n-1} \right) = \emptyset. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a statement in the plane.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: But this follows from the geometry of $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Note that we need the sets $B_{\mathbb R^2_\infty}$ to be open, which is fine.
nodes.statement_short: Plane geometry of dyadic centres.

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centers are separated
nodes.statement: For all $n \geq 3$ the set \[ A:= \{S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0) \,:\, \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}\} \] is $2^{-n+2}$-separated (note: $2^{-n+2} = 4 \cdot 2^{-n}$, which is needed for the construction).
conclusions: is $2^{-n+2}$-separated

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: As shown in the previous lemma, the image of $A$ under $\pi$ is precisely the centers of the dyadic subcubes of $[0,1]$ of level $n-3$. Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$. Then \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}. \] Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$. Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$, where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether the projections differ: horizontal separation of dyadic centers, or vertical separation of 4-adic centers.

nodes.name: Recall projection
nodes.statement: As shown in the previous lemma, the image of $A$ under $\pi$ is precisely the centers of the dyadic subcubes of $[0,1]$ of level $n-3$.
nodes.statement_short: Projections are dyadic centres.

nodes.name: Case different projections
nodes.statement: Let $x,y \in A$ and suppose $\pi(x) \neq \pi(y)$. Then \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \|\pi(x) - \pi(y)\| \geq 2^{-n+3}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Different projections: horizontal separation.

nodes.name: Case same projection
nodes.statement: Now suppose $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ but $x \neq y$. Then as the vertical component of the iterated function system can be viewed independently, we see that the $z$-coordinate of $x$ and $y$ are points in the center of the level $n-3$ 4-dic subintervals of $[\varphi(\pi(x)),\varphi(\pi(x))+1]$, where $\varphi$ is the function in \eqref{eq:phidef}. Thus, they differ by no less than $4^{-n+3}$ and so \[ d_b(x,y) \geq \sqrt{4^{-n+3}} = 2^{-n+3}>2^{-n+2} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Same projection: vertical 4-adic separation.

nodes.name: Level n shortcut centers cover K
nodes.statement: There exists some absolute constant $c_E > 0$ so that \begin{equation} K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3. \end{equation}
conclusions: There exists some absolute constant $c_E > 0$ so that
nodes.label: lma:K-c1

nodes.name: Covering of K by balls (5.4)
nodes.statement: K \subseteq \bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}), \qquad \forall n \geq 3.
nodes.label: e:K-ball-ind

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction. As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough. Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$. Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get \begin{eqnarray*} K& = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\ & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1}) \end{eqnarray*} Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $n$ using the self-similarity $K=\bigcup S_i(K)$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction. As $K$ is bounded, we easily get \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} for $n=3$ by choosing some $c_E$ large enough.
nodes.statement_short: Base case $n=3$ by boundedness of $K$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Now assume that \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for some $n \ge 3$. Then by the self-similarity of $K$ as exhibited in \eqref{e:K-self-similar} we get \begin{eqnarray*} K& = & \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(K) \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{16} S_i(\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-3}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n}))\\ & = &\bigcup_{\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^{n-2}} B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(\frac12,\frac12,0),c_E 2^{-n-1}) \end{eqnarray*} Thus \eqref{e:K-ball-ind} holds for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via $K=\bigcup S_i(K)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 1: (H,d_b) looks down on (K,d)
nodes.statement: By Remark~\ref{rmk:zerocost} taking zero costs for shortcuts is allowed. From the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} we see that $\lambda = \frac12$ works in the Heisenberg group. Now the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold for the constructed distance $d$. That is, the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz, but not biLipschitz on any set of positive measure, and the space $(K,d)$ is Ahlfors regular. In particular, $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$. In order to show that $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ is not minimal in looking down, we still need to prove that $(K,d)$ is a BPI space and that $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1.3 to the self-similar zero-cost shortcuts on $K$: the identity is Lipschitz but nowhere biLipschitz, so $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Hypotheses hold
nodes.statement: By Remark~\ref{rmk:zerocost} taking zero costs for shortcuts is allowed. From the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance} we see that $\lambda = \frac12$ works in the Heisenberg group.
nodes.statement_short: Zero costs are allowed and $\lambda=1/2$ works.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 1.3
nodes.statement: Now the conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:general} hold for the constructed distance $d$. That is, the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K,d_b) \to (K,d)$ is Lipschitz, but not biLipschitz on any set of positive measure, and the space $(K,d)$ is Ahlfors regular.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1.3 to $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Looks down
nodes.statement: In particular, $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ looks down on $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Remaining tasks
nodes.statement: In order to show that $(\mathbb H,d_b)$ is not minimal in looking down, we still need to prove that $(K,d)$ is a BPI space and that $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining: $(K,d)$ is BPI and does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 holds in (K,d)
nodes.statement: Note that Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} holds in $(K,d)$ as its proof, as well as the proof of Lemma~\ref{lma:weak-id}, only require that $\mathcal{N}_{n+1} \cap B_{d_b}(\mathcal{N}_n,4 \lambda^n) = \emptyset$, which holds for the construction of $(K,d)$.
conclusions: Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} holds in $(K,d)$

nodes.name: Short walks next to low-level shortcuts
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ and $n = \min \{k \in \mathbb N : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}$. There exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$, and for any $j \in \mathbb N$ such that $\min (L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}),L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})) = m < n$, then \[ d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \leq 2 \lambda^m. \]
nodes.statement_short: Itineraries in ${\mathcal I}^*$ can be modified so that walks adjacent to level-$m$ shortcuts have length at most $2\lambda^m$.
assumptions: Let ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ and $n = \min \{k \in \mathbb N : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}$.
conclusions: There exists ${\bf x}' \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}')$, $c({\bf x}') \leq c({\bf x})$
nodes.label: lma:small-walks

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_{\bf x}$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$. Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$. Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$. Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$. If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality. Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in ${\bf x}$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points. We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary ${\bf x}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Long walks next to a shortcut let one bypass it via (1.1), lowering cost; iterate.

nodes.name: WLOG
nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that there exist $k \in L^{-1}(n)$ such that $k \geq 2j+1$, that is, $L_{\bf x}$ is still decreasing from $2j-1$ to $2j+1$. Thus, $L(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2}) = m$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG the level function is still decreasing at $j$.

nodes.name: Shortcut centre
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \mathcal{N}_m$ be the point for which the shortcut $(x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2})$ is found in $B_{d_b}(x,\lambda^m)$. Then as $L(x_{2j+3},x_{2j+4}) \leq m$, we get that $x_{2j+3} \notin B(x, \lambda^m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the centre of the level-$m$ shortcut; the next walk ends outside its ball.

nodes.name: Bypass
nodes.statement: If $d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) > 2\lambda^m$, then we get that $x_{2j} \notin B(x,\lambda^m)$ by the triangle inequality. Thus, applying \eqref{e:general-metric-assumption} with $q_1 = x_{2j+1}$, $q_2 = x_{2j+2}$, $p_1 = x_{2j}$, and $p_2 = x_{2j+3}$, we get that we can replace $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1},x_{2j+2},x_{2j+3})$ in ${\bf x}$ with $(x_{2j},x_{2j+3})$ to get a itinerary in ${\mathcal I}^*$ with lower cost and two fewer points with the same extremal points.
nodes.statement_short: A long walk lets (1.1) bypass the shortcut at lower cost.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: We then iterate this procedure until we cannot to get our needed itinerary ${\bf x}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate until done.

nodes.name: Length |i| of a multi-index
nodes.statement: In this section we write $|\mathtt{i}|=k$ if $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$.

nodes.name: Near-optimal itineraries stay near S_i(K)
nodes.statement: There exists some $C > 0$ so that for all multi-indices ${\mathtt{i}}$, for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_n\in B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|})$.
nodes.statement_short: Points of $S_{\mathtt i}(K)$ are joined by near-optimal itineraries staying within $C2^{-|\mathtt i|}$ of $S_{\mathtt i}(K)$.
assumptions: for all multi-indices ${\mathtt{i}}$, for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and all $\epsilon > 0$
conclusions: there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_n\in B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|})$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement:
We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \mathbb N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary ${ f x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that  egin{enumerate} \item $c({ f x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\mathrm{Ext}({ f x}) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad  orall k \in \mathbb N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_{ f x}^{-1}(k) 
eq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${ f x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({ f x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({ f x}) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$. The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$. Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~ef{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \mathbb N$ be the minimal even number such that  egin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and  egin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation} As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that  egin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation} By an application of Lemma~ef{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary ${ f x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. We then apply Lemma~ef{lma:small-walks} on ${ f x}$ (and still calling the result ${ f x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied. Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$. Then \[ c({ f x}) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] a contradiction. Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied. Now suppose $L_{ f x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) 
eq \emptyset$. Suppose first that $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$. Then as ${ f x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) 
otin {\mathcal S}$ such that \[ c({ f x}) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] which is a contradiction. Now suppose that $\# L_{{ f x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$. Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$. Then we have by the triangle inequality  egin{multline*} d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \ - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*). \end{multline*} We have that  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} 
otag \ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray} Together with the fourth property, we get that \[ (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}. \] But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove a six-property claim for deep multi-indices by contradiction on long walks and low-level shortcuts; shallow indices are finitely many.

nodes.name: Claim and reduction
nodes.statement: We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \mathbb N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate} If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$. The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: A six-property claim for deep multi-indices implies the lemma.

nodes.name: State claim
nodes.statement: We claim that there exists some constant $M \in \mathbb N$ depending only on $c_E > 0$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1} such that if $\epsilon > 0$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, and $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, then there exists some itinerary ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, \item $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, \item $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}(k) \leq 4, \qquad \forall k \in \mathbb N$, \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{1-m}$ for all $j$ odd such that \[ m = \min(L(x_{j-2},x_{j-1}),L(x_j,x_{j+1})) < \min \{k : L_{\bf x}^{-1}(k) \neq \emptyset\}, \] \item $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \leq 2^{M/2-k}$ for all $j$ odd, \item $L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M]) = \emptyset$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: State the six properties.

nodes.name: Length bound
nodes.statement: If the claim holds, then we get that for all $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ with $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ for $k \geq M$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and \[ \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} d_b(x_i,x_{i+1}) \leq C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} \] for some $C$ depending on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: The claim bounds the total $d_b$-length of the itinerary by $C2^{-|\mathtt i|}$.

nodes.name: Lemma follows
nodes.statement: The lemma now follows for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k \geq M$ from the triangle inequality and for all $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$ with $k < M$ by the fact that there are only finitely many such $\mathtt{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality for deep indices; finitely many shallow ones.

nodes.name: Prove claim, first part
nodes.statement: Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \mathbb N$ be the minimal even number such that \begin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and \begin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation} As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that \begin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation} By an application of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. We then apply Lemma~\ref{lma:small-walks} on ${\bf x}$ (and still calling the result ${\bf x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Set up $M$ and get properties 1-4 from Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4.

nodes.name: Choose M
nodes.statement: Let us prove the claim. Let $c_E > 0$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:K-c1}. Let $M \in \mathbb N$ be the minimal even number such that \begin{equation} 2^{M/2} > 2c_E \end{equation} and \begin{equation} 2^{M-1} - 2^{M/2+1} - 2^{M/2+7} > c_E 2^{-2}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Diameter bound
nodes.statement: As $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$, if $|\mathtt{i}|=k>M$, we get that \begin{equation} d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Diameter bound (5.7).

nodes.name: Diameter bound in S_i(K) (5.7)
nodes.statement: d(x,y) \leq d_b(x,y) \leq c_E2^{-k}.
nodes.label: e:K-c1-defn

nodes.name: Properties 1-4
nodes.statement: By an application of Lemma~\ref{lma:multiplicity} on some itinerary with cost no more than $(1+\epsilon)d(x,y)$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ that satisfies the first three properties. We then apply Lemma~\ref{lma:small-walks} on ${\bf x}$ (and still calling the result ${\bf x}$) to get that the fourth property is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.3 and 5.4 give properties 1-4.

nodes.name: Property 5
nodes.statement: Suppose $d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) > 2^{M/2-k}$ for some odd $j$. Then \[ c({\bf x}) \geq d_b(x_{j-1},x_j) \geq 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] a contradiction. Thus, the fifth condition is satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: A long walk would cost more than $2d(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Property 6, case >= 2
nodes.statement: Now suppose $L_{\bf x}^{-1}([0,k-M]) \neq \emptyset$. Suppose first that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) \geq 2$. Then as ${\bf x} \in {\mathcal I}^*$, there exists some $(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \notin {\mathcal S}$ such that \[ c({\bf x}) \geq c(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) \geq 4 \cdot 2^{M/2-k} \overset{\eqref{e:K-c1-defn} \wedge \eqref{e:M/2-defn-1}}{>} 2 d(x,y), \] which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Two low-level shortcuts force a long walk: contradiction.

nodes.name: Property 6, case = 1
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $\# L_{{\bf x}}^{-1}([0,k-M/2]) = 1$. Let $L(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) \geq k-M$. Then we have by the triangle inequality \begin{multline*} d_b(x,y) \geq d_b(x_{2j-1},x_{2j}) - \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) - d_b(x_{2j-2},x_{2j-1}) \\ - d_b(x_{2j},x_{2j+1}) - \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^\infty d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) = (*). \end{multline*} We have that \begin{eqnarray} \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} \notag \\ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}. \end{eqnarray} Together with the fourth property, we get that \[ (*) \overset{\eqref{e:small-tails}}{\geq} 2^{M-k-1} - 2^{M/2-k+1} - 2^{M/2-k+7} \overset{\eqref{e:M/2-defn-2}}{>} c_E 2^{-2-k}. \] But this is a contradiction because $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$ and so $d_b(x,y) \leq c_E 2^{-2-k}$.
nodes.statement_short: One low-level shortcut forces $d_b(x,y)$ too large: contradiction.

nodes.name: Small tails (5.8)
nodes.statement: \sum_{\ell=0}^{2j-3} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6} \notag \\ \sum_{\ell=2j+1}^{\infty} d_b(x_\ell,x_{\ell+1}) &\leq& 16 \sum_{s=k-M/2}^\infty 2^{-s} = 2^{M/2-k + 6}.
nodes.label: e:small-tails

nodes.name: Optimal itineraries inside S_i(K) on a sub-piece
nodes.statement: There exists some multi-index $\mathtt{j}$ such that the following property holds. For any $\epsilon > 0$, $k \in \mathbb N$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, and any two $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_N \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
assumptions: For any $\epsilon > 0$, $k \in \mathbb N$, $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, and any two $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$
conclusions: There exists some multi-index $\mathtt{j}$ such that the following property holds.
there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ with $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and $x_0,\dots,x_N \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$.
nodes.label: lma:j-defn

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.6
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma. As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$. As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K. \] Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$. Then there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of ${\bf x}$ is contained \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K). \]
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\mathtt j$ with $S_{\mathtt j}(K)$ deep inside an interior ball of $K$, then rescale Lemma 5.5.

nodes.name: Choose j
nodes.statement: Let $C > 0$ be the constant from the previous lemma. As $K$ has nonempty interior we may choose $x \in \mathrm{int}(K)$ and $h > 0$ so that $B_{d_b}(x,h) \subset K$. As $K$ is compact, there then exists some $\mathtt{j}$ so that \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|}) \subseteq B_{d_b}(x,h) \subseteq K. \]
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\mathtt j$ with the $C2^{-|\mathtt j|}$-neighbourhood of $S_{\mathtt j}(K)$ inside $K$.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.5
nodes.statement: Now let $x,y \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$ for some arbitrary $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$. Then there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_n) \in {\mathcal I}^*$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(x,y)$, $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf x}) = (x,y)$, and each of the points of ${\bf x}$ is contained \[ B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)),C 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|-|\mathtt{j}|}) = S_{\mathtt{i}}(B_{d_b}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K),C 2^{-|\mathtt{j}|})) \subseteq S_{\mathtt{i}}(K). \]
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.5 itinerary stays in the rescaled neighbourhood, inside $S_{\mathtt i}(K)$.

nodes.name: Similitudes scale d exactly on S_j(K)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathtt{j}$ be from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}. Then for all $k \in \mathbb N$ and $\mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k$, we have that \begin{equation} d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K). \end{equation}
conclusions: \begin{equation} d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Exact scaling of d (5.9)
nodes.statement: d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y \in S_{\mathtt{j}}(K).
nodes.label: e:j-invariance

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.7
nodes.statement: If ${\bf x}$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$ by the properties of the shortcuts. Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$. For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$. Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to ${\bf x}$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$. Thus, \[ d(x,y) \leq c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x}) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)). \] Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Similitudes map shortcuts to shortcuts, giving $\le$; Lemma 5.6 gives itineraries inside $S_{\mathtt i}(K)$ to pull back for $\ge$.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: If ${\bf x}$ is an itinerary from $x$ to $y$, then $S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})$ is an itinerary from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ with $c(S_{\mathtt{i}}({\bf x})) = 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$ by the properties of the shortcuts. Thus, we get that $d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)) \leq 2^{-|\mathtt{i}|} d(x,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Images of itineraries give the upper bound.

nodes.name: Lower bound
nodes.statement: For any $\epsilon > 0$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y) \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K))$, we get from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn} that there exists an itinerary ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ from $S_{\mathtt{i}}(x)$ to $S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)$ such that $c({\bf x}) \leq (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y))$ and $x_j \in S_{\mathtt{i}}(K)$. Thus, applying $S_{\mathtt{i}}^{-1}$ to ${\bf x}$, we get an itinerary ${\bf x}'$ from $x$ to $y$ such that $x_j' \in K$ and $c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x})$. Thus, \[ d(x,y) \leq c({\bf x}') = 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} c({\bf x}) \leq 2^{|\mathtt{i}|} (1+\epsilon) d(S_{\mathtt{i}}(x),S_{\mathtt{i}}(y)). \] Taking $\epsilon \to 0$ then gives the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back a Lemma 5.6 itinerary for the lower bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 2: (K,d) is BPI
nodes.statement: We can now prove that $K$ is BPI. Let $\mathtt{j}$ be the multi-index from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}, $p_1,p_2 \in K$, and $0 < r_1,r_2 < \operatorname{diam}(K)$. Now there exist two multi-indices $\mathtt{i_1},\mathtt{i_2}$ such that $\operatorname{diam}(S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K)) \ge c r_j$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K) \subset B(p_j,r_j)$ for $j \in \{1,2\}$. Define $A = S_{\mathtt{i_1}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)) \subset B(p_1,r_1)$. Then the map $f \colon A \to B(p_2,r_2)$ defined as $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2}\circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$ satisfies \[ d(f(p),f(q)) \overset{\eqref{e:j-invariance}}{=} 2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q \in A. \] Since $\mathcal{H}_d^4(A) \ge c\mathcal{H}_d^4(B(p_1,r_1))$ for some $c$ depending only on $\mathtt{j}$ and $2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}$ is comparable to $r_2/r_1$, we are done with showing that $(K,d)$ is BPI.
nodes.statement_short: Compose similitudes $S_{\mathtt i_2}\circ S_{\mathtt i_1}^{-1}$ on $S_{\mathtt i_1}(S_{\mathtt j}(K))$, a similarity for $d$ by Lemma 5.7.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: We can now prove that $K$ is BPI. Let $\mathtt{j}$ be the multi-index from Lemma~\ref{lma:j-defn}, $p_1,p_2 \in K$, and $0 < r_1,r_2 < \operatorname{diam}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\mathtt j$, centres and radii.

nodes.name: Choose pieces
nodes.statement: Now there exist two multi-indices $\mathtt{i_1},\mathtt{i_2}$ such that $\operatorname{diam}(S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K)) \ge c r_j$ and $S_{\mathtt{i}_j}(K) \subset B(p_j,r_j)$ for $j \in \{1,2\}$. Define $A = S_{\mathtt{i_1}}(S_{\mathtt{j}}(K)) \subset B(p_1,r_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick pieces $S_{\mathtt i_j}(K)$ of comparable size inside the balls and set $A$.

nodes.name: Similarity
nodes.statement: Then the map $f \colon A \to B(p_2,r_2)$ defined as $f = S_{\mathtt{i}_2}\circ S_{\mathtt{i}_1}^{-1}$ satisfies \[ d(f(p),f(q)) \overset{\eqref{e:j-invariance}}{=} 2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}d(p,q), \qquad \forall p,q \in A. \]
nodes.statement_short: By (5.9) the composed similitude scales $d$ exactly.

nodes.name: Conclude BPI
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{H}_d^4(A) \ge c\mathcal{H}_d^4(B(p_1,r_1))$ for some $c$ depending only on $\mathtt{j}$ and $2^{|\mathtt{i}_1|-|\mathtt{i}_2|}$ is comparable to $r_2/r_1$, we are done with showing that $(K,d)$ is BPI.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is big and the scale is comparable to $r_2/r_1$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1, part 3: (K,d) does not look down on (H,d_b)
nodes.statement: By contradiction, suppose that $(K,d)$ does look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$. Then there would exist a closed set $A \subset K$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon (A,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\mathcal{H}^4(f(A))>0$. Since $d \le d_b$, also $f \colon (A,d_b) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ is $L$-Lipschitz. Then $f$ is Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere in $A$. Moreover, the Pansu-differential $Df(x)$ is bijective on a set $A' \subset A$ of positive measure by the area formula: \[ 0 < \mathcal{H}^4(f(A)) \overset{\eqref{e:area-formula}}{\le} \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \] Since for all $n,m \in \mathbb N$ the set \[ B_{n,m} = K \setminus \bigcup_{k = n}^\infty \bigcup_{ \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k}S_{\mathtt{i}}(K\cap B_{d_b}(0,\frac1m)) \] has $\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}$-measure zero as a porous set, the set \begin{equation} A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m} \end{equation} has positive measure. Let $x \in A''$ be a density point of $A''$. Since $x \in A''$, by the definition \eqref{eq:Adef} there exists a sequence $(n_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ of integers with $n_m \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ and a sequence of multi-indices $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $|\mathtt{i}_m| = n_m$ such that $x \in S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(K)$ for all $m \in \mathbb N$ and \[ d_b(x,x_m)< \frac1m 2^{-{n_m}} , \] for all $m \in \mathbb N$, where $x_m = S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$. Let $K_m = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(x^{-1}A)\cap K$. Then the functions $f_m \colon (K_m,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ defined as \[ f_m(p) = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))) \] satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & = d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\ & = 2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\ & \le 2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\ & \le L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\ & = L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\ & \le L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the first inequality follows from the fact that $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and the second inequality from the fact that \[ S_{\mathtt{i}_n}({\mathcal S}) \subset {\mathcal S}. \] Notice that \begin{equation} d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0 \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$ since $d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x),0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. The convergence in \eqref{eq:errorterm} holds uniformly for $p \in K$ by the compactness of $K$. Since $x$ is a density point of $A''$ and hence of $A$, we have that for all $p \in K$ there exists a sequence $(p_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ with $p_m \in K_{n_m}$ and $d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. Along this sequence by the fact that $Df(x)$ is homogeneous we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) & = & d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_{n_m}))),\delta_{2^{{n_m}}}(Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))))\\ &=&2^{n_m} d_b(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m)),Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))) \to 0, \end{eqnarray*} as $m \to \infty$. Hence also \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$. Combining the estimates \eqref{eq:fmdestimate}, \eqref{eq:fm_estimate} and \eqref{eq:errorterm} with the fact that $d(p_m,p) \leq d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(Df(x)(p),Df(x)(q)) & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{5.7cm}+ d_b(f_m(p_m),f_m(q_m))\\ & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{0.7cm}+ L\left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p_m,p_m) + d(q_m,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q_m)\right)\\ & &\hspace{3.59cm} + L\left(d(p_m,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,q_m)\right)\\ & \rightarrow & L d(p,q), \qquad \text{as }m \to \infty. \end{eqnarray*} Hence $Df(x)$ is also Lipschitz from $(K,d)$ to $(\mathbb H, d_b)$. Since $Df(x) \colon (\mathbb H, d_b) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is biLipschitz, also the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K, d) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is Lipschitz, but we have shown that this is not the case in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance}.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: blowing up a Lipschitz map at a density point gives a bijective Pansu derivative Lipschitz on $(K,d)$. Then the identity $(K,d)\to(\mathbb H,d_b)$ would be Lipschitz, contradicting Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Assume look down
nodes.statement: By contradiction, suppose that $(K,d)$ does look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$. Then there would exist a closed set $A \subset K$ and a Lipschitz map $f \colon (A,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ with $\mathcal{H}^4(f(A))>0$. Since $d \le d_b$, also $f \colon (A,d_b) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ is $L$-Lipschitz.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Assume a Lipschitz map from closed $A\subset K$ with positive-measure image.

nodes.name: Pansu and area formula
nodes.statement: Then $f$ is Pansu-differentiable almost everywhere in $A$. Moreover, the Pansu-differential $Df(x)$ is bijective on a set $A' \subset A$ of positive measure by the area formula: \[ 0 < \mathcal{H}^4(f(A)) \overset{\eqref{e:area-formula}}{\le} \int_A J(Df(x))\,d\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}(x). \]
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Pansu differentiability and the area formula give bijective derivatives on $A'$.

nodes.name: Set A''
nodes.statement: Since for all $n,m \in \mathbb N$ the set \[ B_{n,m} = K \setminus \bigcup_{k = n}^\infty \bigcup_{ \mathtt{i} \in \{1,\dots,16\}^k}S_{\mathtt{i}}(K\cap B_{d_b}(0,\frac1m)) \] has $\mathcal{H}^4_{d_b}$-measure zero as a porous set, the set \begin{equation} A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m} \end{equation} has positive measure.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Remove porous null sets to get $A''$ of positive measure.

nodes.name: Set A'' (5.10)
nodes.statement: A'' = A' \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \bigcup_{m=1}^\infty B_{n,m}
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.label: eq:Adef

nodes.name: Density point
nodes.statement: Let $x \in A''$ be a density point of $A''$. Since $x \in A''$, by the definition \eqref{eq:Adef} there exists a sequence $(n_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ of integers with $n_m \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$ and a sequence of multi-indices $\mathtt{i}_m$ with $|\mathtt{i}_m| = n_m$ such that $x \in S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(K)$ for all $m \in \mathbb N$ and \[ d_b(x,x_m)< \frac1m 2^{-{n_m}} , \] for all $m \in \mathbb N$, where $x_m = S_{\mathtt{i}_m}(0)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Take a density point $x$ near similitude images of $0$.

nodes.name: Rescaled maps
nodes.statement: Let $K_m = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(x^{-1}A)\cap K$. Then the functions $f_m \colon (K_m,d) \to (\mathbb H,d_b)$ defined as \[ f_m(p) = \delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))) \] satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & = d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\ & = 2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\ & \le 2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\ & \le L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\ & = L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\ & \le L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the first inequality follows from the fact that $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and the second inequality from the fact that \[ S_{\mathtt{i}_n}({\mathcal S}) \subset {\mathcal S}. \]
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Rescaled maps $f_m$ satisfy (5.11).

nodes.name: Estimate for rescaled maps f_m (5.11)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p),f_m(q)) & = d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p))),\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))) \\ & = 2^{n_m} d_b(f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))) \\ & \le 2^{n_m} L d(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p),x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q))\\ & \le L d(S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p)),S_{\mathtt{i}_m}^{-1}(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(q)))\\ & = L d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\\ & \le L \left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q)\right), \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.label: eq:fm_estimate

nodes.name: Error term
nodes.statement: Notice that \begin{equation} d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0 \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$ since $d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x),0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. The convergence in \eqref{eq:errorterm} holds uniformly for $p \in K$ by the compactness of $K$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: The error term (5.12) tends to zero uniformly.

nodes.name: Error term (5.12)
nodes.statement: d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \le d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p,p) \to 0
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.label: eq:errorterm

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: Since $x$ is a density point of $A''$ and hence of $A$, we have that for all $p \in K$ there exists a sequence $(p_m)_{m=1}^\infty$ with $p_m \in K_{n_m}$ and $d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$. Along this sequence by the fact that $Df(x)$ is homogeneous we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) & = & d_b(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_{n_m}))),\delta_{2^{{n_m}}}(Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))))\\ &=&2^{n_m} d_b(f(x)^{-1}f(x\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m)),Df(x)(\delta_{2^{-{n_m}}}(p_m))) \to 0, \end{eqnarray*} as $m \to \infty$. Hence also \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0, \end{aligned} \end{equation} as $m \to \infty$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: $f_m$ converges to $Df(x)$ along approximating sequences.

nodes.name: Convergence to the Pansu derivative (5.13)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) & \le d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p_m)) + d_b(Df(x)(p_m),Df(x)(p)) \to 0, \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.label: eq:fmdestimate

nodes.name: Df(x) Lipschitz
nodes.statement: Combining the estimates \eqref{eq:fmdestimate}, \eqref{eq:fm_estimate} and \eqref{eq:errorterm} with the fact that $d(p_m,p) \leq d_b(p_m,p) \to 0$ we get \begin{eqnarray*} d_b(Df(x)(p),Df(x)(q)) & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{5.7cm}+ d_b(f_m(p_m),f_m(q_m))\\ & \le & d_b(f_m(p_m),Df(x)(p)) + d_b(f_m(q_m),Df(x)(q)) \\ & & \hspace{0.7cm}+ L\left(d(\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)p_m,p_m) + d(q_m,\delta_{2^{n_m}}(x_m^{-1}x)q_m)\right)\\ & &\hspace{3.59cm} + L\left(d(p_m,p) + d(p,q) + d(q,q_m)\right)\\ & \rightarrow & L d(p,q), \qquad \text{as }m \to \infty. \end{eqnarray*} Hence $Df(x)$ is also Lipschitz from $(K,d)$ to $(\mathbb H, d_b)$.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: Hence $Df(x)$ is Lipschitz from $(K,d)$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Since $Df(x) \colon (\mathbb H, d_b) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is biLipschitz, also the identity map $\operatorname{id} \colon (K, d) \to (\mathbb H, d_b)$ is Lipschitz, but we have shown that this is not the case in Theorem \ref{thm:Heisenbergdistance}.
nodes.section: 5.4 $(K,d)$ does not look down on $(\mathbb H,d_b)$
nodes.statement_short: The identity would be Lipschitz, contradicting Theorem 1.2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: Since $ d_{cc}$ is biLipschitz equivalent to the box distance, up to multiplying $d$ by a constant we assume that $d \le d_{b}$. Using the Baire Category Theorem one can show that there exists $L>1$ such that, if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant, see \cite[Lemma 6.7]{LeDonne1}. Suppose that the claim of the theorem is not true. Hence, by the left-biLipschitz invariance of the distances, for all $N\in \mathbb N $ there exists a point $p \in B_{d_b}(0,\frac1{2N})$ with $d_b(0,p) > LN d(0,p)$. Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) . \end{eqnarray}� Indeed, if $q\in B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then \begin{eqnarray*} d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\ &\leq & LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q) \\ &\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2 < 2r_N. \end{eqnarray*} Moreover, for $i < j<N$, we have that \[ d_b(p^i,p^j) = d_b(0,p^{j-i}) \geq d_b(0,p) = r_N. \] Let $\{q_i\}_{i \in I_N}$ be a maximal $4r_N$-separated net of points with respect to distance $d$ in $B_{d_b}(0,1)$. First, by \eqref{ciccio} for all $i \in I_N$ we have that $ \{B_{d_b}(q_i p^n,\frac12 r_N) \}_{n=0}^{N} $ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $ B_{d_b}(q_i,2r_N) $. Second, $\{B_d(q_i,2r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $B_{d_b}(0,2)$. Hence \[ \#I_N N \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N)) \leq \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2)) . \] Since $\{B_d(q_i,8r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ covers $B_{d_b}(0,1)$, by definition of Hausdorff measure we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal{H}_d^4(B_{d_b}(0,1)) & \le & \liminf_{N \to \infty} \#I_N (16r_N)^4\\ &\le& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))}{N\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))} (16r_N)^4\\ & =& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{64^4}{N} = 0. \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts the assumption $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{d_b}(0,1))> 0$.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: short $d$-steps $p$ give $N$ disjoint $d_b$-balls inside one $d$-ball, forcing $\mathcal H^4_d(B_{d_b}(0,1))=0$.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: Since $ d_{cc}$ is biLipschitz equivalent to the box distance, up to multiplying $d$ by a constant we assume that $d \le d_{b}$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize to $d\le d_b$.

nodes.name: Uniform invariance
nodes.statement: Using the Baire Category Theorem one can show that there exists $L>1$ such that, if we restrict to a compact set, then the distance $d$ is $L$-biLipschitz invariant, see \cite[Lemma 6.7]{LeDonne1}.
nodes.statement_short: By Baire category, left translations are uniformly $L$-biLipschitz on compacts.

nodes.name: Assume failure
nodes.statement: Suppose that the claim of the theorem is not true. Hence, by the left-biLipschitz invariance of the distances, for all $N\in \mathbb N $ there exists a point $p \in B_{d_b}(0,\frac1{2N})$ with $d_b(0,p) > LN d(0,p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise there are $p$ near $0$ with $d_b(0,p)>LNd(0,p)$.

nodes.name: Claim (6.1)
nodes.statement: Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) . \end{eqnarray}� Indeed, if $q\in B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then \begin{eqnarray*} d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\ &\leq & LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q) \\ &\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2 < 2r_N. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Claim (6.1): the balls around powers $p^n$ lie in a $d$-ball of radius $2r_N$.

nodes.name: State claim
nodes.statement: Write $r_N := d_b(0,p)>0$. We claim that we have that \begin{eqnarray} \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Set $r_N$ and state (6.1).

nodes.name: Chain of balls inside a d-ball (6.1)
nodes.statement: \bigcup_{n=0}^{N}B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N) \subset B_d(0,2 r_N) .
nodes.label: ciccio

nodes.name: Verify claim
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $q\in B_{d_b}(p^n,\frac12 r_N)$, for some $n\leq N$, then \begin{eqnarray*} d(0,q) & \leq &d(0,p) + d(p,p^2)+\ldots + d(p^{n-1} , p^n) + d(p^n , q)\\ &\leq & LN d(0,p) + d_b(p^n , q) \\ &\leq & d_b(0,p) + r_N/2 < 2r_N. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain along powers of $p$.

nodes.name: Separation of powers
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $i < j<N$, we have that \[ d_b(p^i,p^j) = d_b(0,p^{j-i}) \geq d_b(0,p) = r_N. \]
nodes.statement_short: Powers of $p$ are $r_N$-separated in $d_b$.

nodes.name: Packing
nodes.statement: Let $\{q_i\}_{i \in I_N}$ be a maximal $4r_N$-separated net of points with respect to distance $d$ in $B_{d_b}(0,1)$. First, by \eqref{ciccio} for all $i \in I_N$ we have that $ \{B_{d_b}(q_i p^n,\frac12 r_N) \}_{n=0}^{N} $ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $ B_{d_b}(q_i,2r_N) $. Second, $\{B_d(q_i,2r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ is a disjointed collection of subsets of $B_{d_b}(0,2)$. Hence \[ \#I_N N \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N)) \leq \mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2)) . \]
nodes.statement_short: Packing bound on $\#I_N$ via disjoint balls.

nodes.name: Covering
nodes.statement: Since $\{B_d(q_i,8r_N)\}_{i \in I_N}$ covers $B_{d_b}(0,1)$, by definition of Hausdorff measure we deduce \begin{eqnarray*} \mathcal{H}_d^4(B_{d_b}(0,1)) & \le & \liminf_{N \to \infty} \#I_N (16r_N)^4\\ &\le& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,2))}{N\mathcal{H}_{d_b}^4(B_{d_b}(0,\frac12 r_N))} (16r_N)^4\\ & =& \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{64^4}{N} = 0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Covering estimate gives $\mathcal H^4_d(B_{d_b}(0,1))=0$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: This contradicts the assumption $\mathcal H^4_{d}(B_{d_b}(0,1))> 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with the measure assumption.

nodes.name: Vertical shortcuts from the origin S_0
nodes.statement: Let us define the set of shortcuts from the origin as \[ {\mathcal S}_0 = \left\{ \left(0,(0,0,4^{-n}) \right) \;:\; n \in a^{-1}(\{1\}) \right\}, \] where $a \colon \mathbb N \to \{0,1\}$ is a function determining whether a shortcut is taken on scale $4^{-n}$.

nodes.name: Left-translated shortcuts and their cost
nodes.statement: The full set of shortcuts is then defined as \[ {\mathcal S} = \left\{ (p q_1, p q_2 )\; : \; p \in \mathbb H , \,(q_1,q_2) \vee (q_2, q_1) \in {\mathcal S}_0 \right\} \] and the cost function $c \colon \mathbb H \times \mathbb H \to [0,\infty)$ for $(p,q) \in {\mathcal S}$ as \[ c(p,q) = \frac12 d_{cc}(p,q). \]

nodes.name: Distance d_1
nodes.statement: The distance $d_1$ is then defined as the $d$ in \eqref{eq:ddef}.

nodes.name: d_1 is a left-invariant distance biLipschitz to d_cc
nodes.statement: Since $\frac12 d_{cc} \le d_1 \le d_{cc}$, the function $d_1$ is a distance and it is biLipschitz equivalent with $d_{cc}$. By the left-invariace of the set of shortcuts ${\mathcal S}$, the distance $d_1$ is also left-invariant.
conclusions: the function $d_1$ is a distance and it is biLipschitz equivalent with $d_{cc}$
the distance $d_1$ is also left-invariant

nodes.name: Shortcut-scale selector function a
nodes.statement: Since we want to avoid self-similarity, we define the function $a$ so that every word written in the alphabets $\{0,1\}$ appears consecutively in the sequence $(a(n))_{n\in\mathbb N}$ only some limited number of times. This is achieved for example by defining \[ a(i) := \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if there exists }k \text{ odd and }l \in \mathbb N\text{ such that }i = (k\ell\prod_{h < \ell}p_h+1)p_\ell\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \] where $p_\ell$ is the $\ell$:th prime number.
nodes.statement_short: $a(i)=1$ iff $i=(k\ell\prod_{h<\ell}p_h+1)p_\ell$ for some odd $k$; no binary word repeats periodically too often.

nodes.name: The sequence a has no long periodic stretches
nodes.statement: Let $\ell \geq 1$. There exists some $m \geq 1$ so that for any $i \geq 1$, there exists some $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.
conclusions: There exists some $m \geq 1$ so that for any $i \geq 1$, there exists some $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $a(j) \neq a(j+m\ell)$.
nodes.label: lma:norepeat

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let us write \[ P_\ell = \left\{(k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\right\}. \] We claim that $\{P_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb N}$ is a disjointed collection of sets. In order to see this take $0 < \ell < \ell'< \infty$ and notice that on one hand for every $k \in \mathbb N$ we have $p_\ell \mid (k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell$. On the other hand, since $p_\ell \mid \prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}$, we have $p_\ell \nmid (k\ell'\prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}+1)p_{\ell'}$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Now let $\ell \geq 1$ be given. Define $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_{h}$. Then $P_\ell = \{p_\ell + m\ell k \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}$. Let $i \ge 1$ and select $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $j \equiv p_\ell \pmod{m\ell}$. Then by definition, $j \in P_\ell$. By the fact that the sets $P_{\ell'}$ are pairwise disjoint we have from the definition of $a$ that \[ a(m\ell k + p_{\ell}) = \begin{cases} 1,& \text{if }k \text{ is odd},\\ 0,& \text{if }k \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \] Thus $a(j) \neq a(j + \ell m)$.
nodes.statement_short: The sets $P_\ell$ are pairwise disjoint (divisibility by primes) and $a$ alternates along the progression $P_\ell$.

nodes.name: Define P_ell
nodes.statement: Let us write \[ P_\ell = \left\{(k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\right\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define the progressions $P_\ell$.

nodes.name: Disjointness claim
nodes.statement: We claim that $\{P_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb N}$ is a disjointed collection of sets. In order to see this take $0 < \ell < \ell'< \infty$ and notice that on one hand for every $k \in \mathbb N$ we have $p_\ell \mid (k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell$. On the other hand, since $p_\ell \mid \prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}$, we have $p_\ell \nmid (k\ell'\prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}+1)p_{\ell'}$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.statement_short: The $P_\ell$ are pairwise disjoint.

nodes.name: Divisibility
nodes.statement: We claim that $\{P_\ell\}_{\ell \in \mathbb N}$ is a disjointed collection of sets. In order to see this take $0 < \ell < \ell'< \infty$ and notice that on one hand for every $k \in \mathbb N$ we have $p_\ell \mid (k\ell \prod_{h < \ell}p_{h}+1)p_\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: State disjointness; $p_\ell$ divides elements of $P_\ell$.

nodes.name: Non-divisibility
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $p_\ell \mid \prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}$, we have $p_\ell \nmid (k\ell'\prod_{h < \ell'}p_{h}+1)p_{\ell'}$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$.
nodes.statement_short: $p_\ell$ divides no element of $P_{\ell'}$.

nodes.name: Choose m
nodes.statement: Now let $\ell \geq 1$ be given. Define $m = \prod_{h \le \ell}p_{h}$. Then $P_\ell = \{p_\ell + m\ell k \,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $m=\prod_{h\le\ell}p_h$ so $P_\ell$ is an arithmetic progression.

nodes.name: Pick j
nodes.statement: Let $i \ge 1$ and select $j \in \{i,i+1,\dots,i + m\ell\}$ such that $j \equiv p_\ell \pmod{m\ell}$. Then by definition, $j \in P_\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $j$ in the window lying in $P_\ell$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By the fact that the sets $P_{\ell'}$ are pairwise disjoint we have from the definition of $a$ that \[ a(m\ell k + p_{\ell}) = \begin{cases} 1,& \text{if }k \text{ is odd},\\ 0,& \text{if }k \text{ is even}. \end{cases} \] Thus $a(j) \neq a(j + \ell m)$.
nodes.statement_short: $a$ alternates along $P_\ell$.

nodes.name: Vertical itineraries suffice
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ be an itinerary such that $x_0 = 0$ and $x_N \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$. Then there exists another itinerary ${\bf y} = (y_0,\dots,y_M)$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf y}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})$, $y_{i+1}^{-1}y_i \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$ for all $i$, and $c({\bf y}) \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.statement_short: An itinerary from $0$ to a central point can be rearranged into one with central increments and no greater cost.
assumptions: Let ${\bf x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$ be an itinerary such that $x_0 = 0$ and $x_N \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$.
conclusions: there exists another itinerary ${\bf y} = (y_0,\dots,y_M)$ such that $\mathrm{Ext}({\bf y}) = \mathrm{Ext}({\bf x})$, $y_{i+1}^{-1}y_i \in {\rm Z}({\mathbb H})$ for all $i$, and $c({\bf y}) \leq c({\bf x})$.
nodes.label: lma:vertical-itinerary

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement:
For the itinerary ${ f x} = (x_0,\dots,x_N)$, we define $d_k = x_i^{-1}x_{i-1}$. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.6
nodes.statement: Assume to the contrary that there exists a sequence $(\lambda_j)_{j \in \mathbb N}$, with $\lambda_j \to 0$ such that the distances $$(p,q)\mapsto \dfrac{1}{\lambda_j} d_1(\delta_{\lambda_j} (p),\delta_{\lambda_j} (q)) $$ converge pointwise to some $\rho$, and the distance $\rho$ is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. Let us now find a contradiction by using the assumed self-similarity. For this purpose let us first take a point $(0,0,s^2) \in \mathbb H$ appearing as limit of points to which there is a shortcut from the origin. In other words, take \begin{equation} s \in [1,2^4] \cap \bigcap_{j=1}^\infty\overline{\bigcup_{i \geq j} \{\lambda_i^{-1}2^{-4(k+1)}\,:\, k \in \mathbb N\}}. \end{equation} Then we indeed have \[ \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda_j^2s^2)) = \frac12d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)), \] since $a(4(k+1))= 1$ for all $k \in \mathbb N$. Let us then use the function $f$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} to show that there exists $\ell \in \mathbb N$ such that $\lambda = 2^\ell$. Supposing this is not the case, we have $\lambda = t2^\ell$ for some $t \in (1,2)$ and $\ell \in \mathbb N$. By \eqref{14598015} $s$ is of the form $s=\lim_{m\to \infty} \lambda_{i_m}^{-1} 2^{-4(k_m+1)}$, with $i_m, k_m\to \infty$. Then, by the continuity of the function $f$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,\lambda^2s^2)) & = &\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &\lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} d_1(0,(0,0, t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2 4^\ell 4^{-4(k_m+1)}\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2)) \\ & \ge& \lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} f\left(t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2\right ) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ &=& f(t^2)\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &f(t^2)\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) > \frac12\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lambda \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) , \end{eqnarray*} contradicting the fact that $\rho$ is self-similar with the dilation $\lambda$. Therefore $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. Now we employ the properties of the function $a$. Let $m \in \mathbb N$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}. Since $\rho$ is self-similar with factor $2^\ell$, it is self-similar also with factor $2^{\ell m}$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformupperbound}, we have that there exists some $\eta$ such that $(1+\eta)^N = 4$ for some $N \in \mathbb N$ and if $a(n) = 1$, then \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})) \leq 0.51 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})), \qquad \forall t \in (-\eta,\eta). \end{equation} Take $j_0 \in \mathbb N$ such that for all $j \ge j_0$ we have \begin{equation} \frac{\rho(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^ks^2))}{\lambda_j^{-1} d_1(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k\lambda_j^2s^2))} \in \left(1 - \frac{1}{100}, 1 + \frac{1}{100} \right), \end{equation} for all $(i,k) \in \{0,1,\dots,2 m\ell\} \times \{0,\dots,N-1\}$. Let $n \in \mathbb Z$ be such that $(\lambda_j s)^2 \in \left[ \frac{1}{2} 4^{-n}, 2 \cdot 4^{-n}\right)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}, we have that there exists some $i \in \{0,\dots,m \ell\}$ such that $a(n+i) \neq a(n+ i + m\ell)$. We may suppose without loss of generality that $a(n+i) = 1$ so $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$. We have that there exists some $k \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ such that $4^i(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in ((1-\eta) 4^{n+i},(1+\eta) 4^{n+i})$. Thus, because $a(n+i) = 1$, we have that \begin{equation} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \overset{\eqref{e:upperbound} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\leq} 0.52 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{equation} On the other hand, because $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$ and $$4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in \left( \frac{1}{2} 4^{n+i+m\ell}, 2 \cdot 4^{n+i+m\ell} \right),$$ we have that \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) &\overset{\eqref{e:sqrt3-lower} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\geq} &\frac{99}{100} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \\ &\geq& 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k s^2)), \\ &=& 0.55 \cdot 2^{m\ell} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} Then by the self-similarity of $\rho$ with ratio $2^{m\ell}$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) & = & 2^{-m\ell}\rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2))\\ & \ge & 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts \eqref{eq:finalcontra}.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: Lemma 6.3 forces the self-similarity factor to be $2^\ell$. Then Lemma 6.1 finds scales $n+i$, $n+i+m\ell$ with different $a$, where Lemmas 6.4 and 6.5 give incompatible ratios.

nodes.statement: Let us then use the function $f$ of Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} to show that there exists $\ell \in \mathbb N$ such that $\lambda = 2^\ell$. Supposing this is not the case, we have $\lambda = t2^\ell$ for some $t \in (1,2)$ and $\ell \in \mathbb N$. By \eqref{14598015} $s$ is of the form $s=\lim_{m\to \infty} \lambda_{i_m}^{-1} 2^{-4(k_m+1)}$, with $i_m, k_m\to \infty$. Then, by the continuity of the function $f$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,\lambda^2s^2)) & = &\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_1(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &\lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} d_1(0,(0,0, t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2 4^\ell 4^{-4(k_m+1)}\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2)) \\ & \ge& \lim_{m \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_{i_m}} f\left(t^2 \left( \dfrac{\lambda_{i_m} s}{ 2^{-4(k_m+1)}}\right)^2\right ) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ &=& f(t^2)\lim_{j \to \infty}\frac{1}{\lambda_j}d_{cc}(0,(0,0,\lambda^2\lambda_j^2s^2))\\ & = &f(t^2)\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) > \frac12\lambda d_{cc}(0,(0,0,s^2)) = \lambda \rho(0,(0,0,s^2)) , \end{eqnarray*} contradicting the fact that $\rho$ is self-similar with the dilation $\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.3 forces $\lambda=2^\ell$.

nodes.name: Use Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Therefore $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. Now we employ the properties of the function $a$. Let $m \in \mathbb N$ be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}. Since $\rho$ is self-similar with factor $2^\ell$, it is self-similar also with factor $2^{\ell m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $m$ from Lemma 6.1; factor $2^{\ell m}$ also works.

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lma:uniformupperbound}, we have that there exists some $\eta$ such that $(1+\eta)^N = 4$ for some $N \in \mathbb N$ and if $a(n) = 1$, then \begin{equation} d_1(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})) \leq 0.51 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})), \qquad \forall t \in (-\eta,\eta). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.5 gives the upper bound (6.9).

nodes.name: Choose scales
nodes.statement: Take $j_0 \in \mathbb N$ such that for all $j \ge j_0$ we have \begin{equation} \frac{\rho(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^ks^2))}{\lambda_j^{-1} d_1(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k\lambda_j^2s^2))} \in \left(1 - \frac{1}{100}, 1 + \frac{1}{100} \right), \end{equation} for all $(i,k) \in \{0,1,\dots,2 m\ell\} \times \{0,\dots,N-1\}$. Let $n \in \mathbb Z$ be such that $(\lambda_j s)^2 \in \left[ \frac{1}{2} 4^{-n}, 2 \cdot 4^{-n}\right)$. By Lemma~\ref{lma:norepeat}, we have that there exists some $i \in \{0,\dots,m \ell\}$ such that $a(n+i) \neq a(n+ i + m\ell)$. We may suppose without loss of generality that $a(n+i) = 1$ so $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $j_0$ for precision (6.10) and scales with $a(n+i)\ne a(n+i+m\ell)$.

nodes.name: Bound at n+i
nodes.statement: We have that there exists some $k \in \{0,\dots,N-1\}$ such that $4^i(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in ((1-\eta) 4^{n+i},(1+\eta) 4^{n+i})$. Thus, because $a(n+i) = 1$, we have that \begin{equation} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \overset{\eqref{e:upperbound} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\leq} 0.52 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound 0.52 at scale $n+i$.

nodes.name: Final contradiction inequality (6.11)
nodes.statement: \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \overset{\eqref{e:upperbound} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\leq} 0.52 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)).
nodes.label: eq:finalcontra

nodes.name: Bound at n+i+ml
nodes.statement: On the other hand, because $a(n+i+m\ell) = 0$ and $$4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k \lambda_j^2 s^2 \in \left( \frac{1}{2} 4^{n+i+m\ell}, 2 \cdot 4^{n+i+m\ell} \right),$$ we have that \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) &\overset{\eqref{e:sqrt3-lower} \wedge \eqref{e:precision}}{\geq} &\frac{99}{100} \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2)) \\ &\geq& 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell}(1+\eta)^k s^2)), \\ &=& 0.55 \cdot 2^{m\ell} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound 0.55 at scale $n+i+m\ell$ via Lemma 6.4.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Then by the self-similarity of $\rho$ with ratio $2^{m\ell}$ we have \begin{eqnarray*} \rho(0,(0,0,4^i (1+\eta)^k s^2)) & = & 2^{-m\ell}\rho(0,(0,0,4^{i+m\ell} (1+\eta)^k s^2))\\ & \ge & 0.55 d_{cc}(0,(0,0,4^i(1+\eta)^k s^2)). \end{eqnarray*} This contradicts \eqref{eq:finalcontra}.
nodes.statement_short: Self-similarity transfers the lower bound: contradiction.

nodes.name: Dyadic centers D_n
nodes.statement: Let $D_n$ denote the centers of the dyadic cubes in $\mathbb R^2$ of sidelength $2^{-n}$.

nodes.name: Level n shortcuts for d_2
nodes.statement: Define the level $n$ shortcuts as the symmetrization of \[ \tilde{\mathcal S}_n = \{((x,y,z),(x,y,z)q) : (x,y) \in D_n, z \in \mathbb R, q = (0,0,\pm 4^{-n})\}. \]

nodes.name: Shortcut set for d_2
nodes.statement: We then construct the set of shortcuts as \[ \tilde{\mathcal S} = \bigcup_{n \in a^{-1}(\{1\})} \tilde{\mathcal S}_n. \]

nodes.name: Cost function for d_2
nodes.statement: As in the construction of $d_1$, the cost function $\tilde c : \mathbb{H} \times \mathbb{H} \to [0,\infty)$ for $(p,q) \in \tilde{\mathcal S}$ is \[ \tilde c(p,q) = \frac{1}{2} d_{cc}(p,q). \]

nodes.name: Distance d_2
nodes.statement: The distance $d_2$ is then obtained as the distance $d$ in \eqref{eq:ddef}, but now with using $\tilde c$.

nodes.name: Comparison of d_1, d_2 and d_cc
nodes.statement: Since $\tilde{\mathcal S} \subset {\mathcal S}$ and thus $\tilde c \ge c$, we have \[ \frac{1}{2} d_{cc} \leq d_1 \leq d_2 \leq d_{cc}. \]
conclusions: \[ \frac{1}{2} d_{cc} \leq d_1 \leq d_2 \leq d_{cc}. \]

nodes.name: Lower bound for d_2 off the dyadic grid
nodes.statement: There exists some absolute $\delta > 0$ so that if for any $n \in \mathbb N$, if $(x,y) \in B(D_n + (2^{-n-1},2^{-n-1}),\delta 2^{-n})$ and $t \in (1/2,2)$, then \[ d_2((x,y,z),(x,y,z + t4^{-n})) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \qquad \forall z \in \mathbb R. \]
conclusions: There exists some absolute $\delta > 0$
\[ d_2((x,y,z),(x,y,z + t4^{-n})) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})), \qquad \forall z \in \mathbb R. \]
nodes.label: l:off-grid

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.7
nodes.statement: Let $(a,b) \in D_n$ be so that $(x,y) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ ($\delta$ to be chosen later) and let ${\bf x} = (x_0,...,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $(x,y,z)$ to $(x,y,z + t4^{-n})$. Note that \[ d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sqrt{t 4^{-n}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n}. \] Suppose first that there is some $\pi(x_j) \notin B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$. As any non-vertical movement is not a shortcut, we have from the fact that $\pi(x_0) = \pi(x_N) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ that if we choose $\delta$ sufficiently small, then \[ c({\bf x}) \geq (1-2\delta) 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})). \] This would prove the statement of the lemma. Thus, we may suppose that the projection of ${\bf x}$ under $\pi$ does not go outside $B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$. But now the proof is reduced to that of the proof of Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-2}. Indeed, by the hypothesis of this subcase, the itinerary ${\bf x}$ cannot contain any level $n$ shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Either the itinerary leaves a horizontal square (costly walk) or it uses no level-$n$ shortcut and the proof of Lemma 6.4 applies.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $(a,b) \in D_n$ be so that $(x,y) \in B((a,b),\delta 2^{-n})$ ($\delta$ to be chosen later) and let ${\bf x} = (x_0,...,x_N)$ be an itinerary from $(x,y,z)$ to $(x,y,z + t4^{-n})$. Note that \[ d_{cc}(0,(0,0,t4^{-n})) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \sqrt{t 4^{-n}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi}} 2^{-n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Nearest dyadic centre and an itinerary; bound $d_{cc}$ of the vertical displacement.

nodes.name: Case leaves square
nodes.statement: Suppose first that there is some $\pi(x_j) \notin B((a,b),2^{-n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Leaving the square costs a long horizontal walk.

nodes.name: Reduce to Lemma 6.4
nodes.statement: But now the proof is reduced to that of the proof of Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-2}. Indeed, by the hypothesis of this subcase, the itinerary ${\bf x}$ cannot contain any level $n$ shortcuts.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise no level-$n$ shortcut is used and Lemma 6.4's proof applies.

nodes.name: Upper bound for d_2 on the dyadic grid
nodes.statement: For every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists $\eta \in (0,1/2)$ so that if $|t| < \eta$ and $a(n) = 1$, then for all $(x,y) \in B(D_n,\eta 2^{-n})$ and $z \in \mathbb R$ we have \[ d_2((x,y,z),(x,y,z + (1+t)4^{-n})) \leq \left( \frac{1}{2} + \epsilon \right) d_{cc}(0,(0,0,(1+t)4^{-n})). \]
conclusions: there exists $\eta \in (0,1/2)$
nodes.label: l:grid-upper

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.8
nodes.statement: This follows by essentially the same proof as Lemma \ref{lma:uniformupperbound}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as the proof of Lemma 6.5.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.5
nodes.statement: Since the shortcuts are horizontally located on the centers of the dyadic cubes, we have from an easy argument using Lemmas \ref{l:off-grid} and \ref{l:grid-upper} that no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant. In order to see that no blow-up of $d_2$ is self-similar we argue similarly as for the distance $d_1$. First suppose that a blow-up is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. This time, instead of finding a limit point $(0,0,s^2)$ of shortcuts from the origin, we find by compactness a pair of points $(x,y,z)$, $(x,y,z + s^2)$ in $B_{d_{cc}}(0,2^5)$ with $s \in [1,2^4]$ appearing as the limit of endpoints of a sequence of shortcuts. This is possible after passing to a subsequence because $a(4(n+1)) = 1$ for all $n$. Observe that Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} holds also for $d_2$ since $d_2 \ge d_1$. As in the case of $d_1$, it then follows via Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} that $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. A contradiction with self-similarity then follows again by the properties of the function $a$. This concludes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fail}.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) is Proposition 6.6 for $d_1$; for $d_2$, Lemmas 6.7-6.8 rule out left-invariance and the $d_1$ argument rules out self-similarity.

nodes.name: Not left-invariant
nodes.statement: Since the shortcuts are horizontally located on the centers of the dyadic cubes, we have from an easy argument using Lemmas \ref{l:off-grid} and \ref{l:grid-upper} that no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 show no blow-up of $d_2$ is left-invariant.

nodes.name: Assume self-similar
nodes.statement: In order to see that no blow-up of $d_2$ is self-similar we argue similarly as for the distance $d_1$. First suppose that a blow-up is self-similar with some constant $\lambda > 1$. This time, instead of finding a limit point $(0,0,s^2)$ of shortcuts from the origin, we find by compactness a pair of points $(x,y,z)$, $(x,y,z + s^2)$ in $B_{d_{cc}}(0,2^5)$ with $s \in [1,2^4]$ appearing as the limit of endpoints of a sequence of shortcuts. This is possible after passing to a subsequence because $a(4(n+1)) = 1$ for all $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a self-similar blow-up of $d_2$ and find by compactness a limit pair of shortcut endpoints.

nodes.name: lambda is a power of 2; conclude
nodes.statement: Observe that Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} holds also for $d_2$ since $d_2 \ge d_1$. As in the case of $d_1$, it then follows via Lemma \ref{lma:uniformlowerbounds-1} that $\lambda = 2^\ell$ for some $\ell \in \mathbb N$. A contradiction with self-similarity then follows again by the properties of the function $a$. This concludes the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:fail}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.3 holds for $d_2\ge d_1$, so $\lambda=2^\ell$; the properties of $a$ then give a contradiction.
